Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Smaller article this week as we take a quick trot around the Francosphere, with a decent almost 80 man sized event in France, followed by a smaller invitational in Quebec for a properly spooky duo of undead factions for Halloween.

The emphasis on Askurgan Trueblades are a huge advantage here for the Soulblight, since the Stormcast decided to go so heavy on Monsters. As before, Sylvaneth's strength is their very large monsters. They're some of the hardest hitting creatures in the game, not always the most durable but if they get a hit in, they can do some serious damage.

Thankfully their Wyldwoods and support heroes exist to grant them buffs like Strike First (or Strike Last on the opponent) and Wards to make them more durable, so the play is to plan out when exactly to strike an opponent while hiding in the trees and rip the enemy apart. title: MTG Commander banlist 2026
content:
Looking for the MTG Commander banlist? Commander is a vast, powerful, and ever-changing format, so it's crucial to stay on top of card bans. If you need a quick reminder of which cards can and can't go in your favorite deck, here's a complete list of Commander bans, from the latest to the very first.

So far, there have been 83 banned cards in MTG's Commander format. Use the links below to check out the latest changes and updates; the full banlist; or Wizards' new system of Game Changers and play brackets in EDH, explained. For more bans in other formats, see our full MTG banlist tracker.

  • Latest Commander banlist update
  • Full Commander banlist
  • Game Changers list
  • Brackets explained

Latest Commander banlist update

On February 9, 2026, Wizards of the Coast unbanned two Commander cards:

  • Biorhythm
  • Lutri, the Spellchaser (except as Companion)

Lutri's case is obvious - it was only banned because it could serve as a Companion in any deck.

The decision to make a new designation 'banned as Companion' appeared to weigh heavily on the designers, based on Gavin Verhey's article - adding sub-lists increases complexity and the chance that players will bring a card in a slot it's not supposed to. The decision was deemed acceptable because the worst case scenario for player mistakes isn't that bad - you tell the player with Lutri in the companion slot that he's banned, and they drop him into the 99.

Because Lutri was banned for reasons not really related to power he bypassed the gamechangers list, where unbanned cards typically go.

Meanwhile, Biorhythm was unbanned following a trend of unbanning expensive, high-impact cards that have a big impact on the game. If Worldfire and Coalition Victory can be legal cards without messing up the format too much, so can Biorhythm.

Full Commander banlist

(8 of) The Power 9

  • Ancestral Recall - banned April 2005
  • Black Lotus - banned April 2005
  • Mox Emerald - banned April 2005
  • Mox Jet - banned April 2005
  • Mox Pearl - banned April 2005
  • Mox Ruby - banned April 2005
  • Mox Sapphire - banned April 2005
  • Time Walk - banned April 2005

It's no surprise to see these here. If any card was going to be banned in Commander, it would be the Power 9 - some of the most broken cards ever made in Magic, each offering absurd value for their mana cost.

Speaking of cost, what's interesting is that it was their price point, not their power level, that originally saw these cards consigned to the Commander banlist - in the very first spate of bannings back in 2005.

The RC was worried that these cards would auto-includes for anyone wanting a really strong deck, and didn't want the fan-made format to have a perceived budget of thousands of dollars.

You might notice only 8/9ths of the Power 9 is actually banned. Timetwister is really an honorary member of the gang - it's busted when played with cards from the other 8. But in fact, a wheel, even a really great wheel like Timetwister, isn't worth making a fuss about.

Broken in the format

  • Limited Resources - banned June 2008
  • Channel - banned April 2005
  • Fastbond - banned June 2009
  • Trade Secrets - banned April 2013
  • Griselbrand - banned June 2012
  • Karakas - banned September 2008
  • Lutri, the Spellchaser - banned as companion February 2026
  • Yawgmoth's Bargain - banned May 2006

These cards are all banned because their designs are unbalanced in the context of EDH. Some, like Channel and Yawgmoth's Bargain, use life as a resource - one that's far more abundant when you start on 40. Others work poorly with multiple players. For instance, Trade Secrets allows two players to collude against the others for a runaway advantage, while Limited Resources stops anyone playing more than two to three lands.

Finally, Lutri is only banned as a companion - because the singleton nature of the format means he could (and therefore, optimally, should) be a companion for any red/blue deck.

It's almost refreshing to see these designs - memories of a time before every card was designed for Commander.

Dexterity cards

  • Chaos Orb - banned June 2010
  • Falling Star - banned April 2005

These feel more like unset cards, and wouldn't be printed without the acorn stamp today. The RC didn't want cards that relied on manual dexterity, so for the sake of both accessibility and convenience, these were banned.

  • Balance - banned April 2005
  • Dockside Extortionist - banned September 2024
  • Emrakul, the Aeons Torn - banned December 2010

  • Recurring Nightmare - banned February 2008
  • Rofellos, Llanowar Emissary - banned September 2014
  • Shahrazad - banned September 2011
  • Sundering Titan - banned June 2012
  • Sylvan Primordial - banned February 2014
  • Time Vault - banned December 2008
  • Tinker - banned March 2009
  • Tolarian Academy - banned June 2010
  • Upheaval - banned April 2005

Conspiracy cards

25 cards with the Conspiracy type are banned in Commander and all other formats. The full list of Conspiracy cards banned in Commander is:

Ante cards

Nine cards that reference 'playing for ante' are banned in Commander and all other formats. This is because they don't work within the rules. Playing for keeps in a four-player game is probably a bad bet anyhow. The banned MTG ante cards are:

  • Amulet of Quoz

Offensive cards

The Commander banlist includes cards that are racially or culturally insensitive. These cards have been banned in all formats, and their images were even removed from Wizards of the Coast's database in 2020. The seven cards currently included in this ban are:

  • Invoke Prejudice
  • Cleanse
  • Stone-Throwing Devils
  • Pradesh Gypsies
  • Jihad
  • Imprison
  • Crusade

Game Changers list

In 2025, Wizards of the Coast introduced a separate but linked 'Game Changers' list to the banlist conversation. Game Changers are cards that dramatically warp a game when (or shortly after) they're played. The number of game changers a deck contains is one factor in determining which Commander 'bracket' it falls into during pre-game discussions.

Though certainly not banned - or even at risk of banning - Wizards has made it clear that future banned cards are likely to come from this list. Similarly, any cards that get unbanned are likely to move onto the Game Changers list.

Wizards of the Coast last updated the Game Changers list along with the latest Commander banlist update on February 9, 2026.

Brackets explained

The beta brackets system is a tool to help Commander players talk about the gameplay experience they want to create with their deck. Each bracket has a set of deck-building conditions: if a deck meets those conditions, it sits in that bracket.

1. Exhibition

Decks prioritize theme over function and showcase a unique idea or experience over valuing winning.

  • No game changers
  • No mass land denial
  • No extra turns
  • No two-card infinite combos (game-enders, lockouts, or infinite)
  • Few tutors

2. Core

Decks are focused, even if every card choice isn't the highest power, and comparable to an average precon. Wins are often telegraphed or incremental.

  • No game changers
  • No mass land denial
  • No chaining extra turns
  • No two-card infinite combos (game-enders, lockouts, or infinite)
  • Few tutors

3. Upgraded

Decks are thoughtfully designed, full of synergistic or strong cards. Games could end out of nowhere with powerful spells and late-game combos.

  • No mass land denial
  • No chaining extra turns
  • Late game, two-card infinite combos allowed
  • Up to three game changers

4. Optimized

Decks are turbocharged with the most powerful cards in the format. Everybody intends to win and is ready to play against anything.

No restrictions other than the banlist.

5. CEDH

Decks are built to win in the competitive metagame. Players intend to use only the most powerful strategies.

  • No restrictions other than the banlist.

Are Commander brackets power levels?

Commander brackets are numbered, but these numbers don't measure the power level of a deck. The higher the bracket, the more tools the deck has to succeed in competitive, meta-focused gameplay. The lower the bracket, the more casual and focused on 'doing something neat with friends' the deck is.

Hopefully, players can use the brackets to choose decks that have similar gameplay goals. There will still be decks that perform well above or below what their bracket suggests.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Shamblerot Vectorium (Updated October 21, 2026)
content:
In our Detachment Focus series we take a deep dive into an army’s Detachments, covering what’s in them, how they play, and how they’ll fit into the broader meta and your games. In this Detachment Focus we’re looking at the Shamblerot Vectorium from the Death Guard.

Night of the Living Dead, 28 Days Later, High School Musical 3: Senior Year. All of these films feature glassy eyed, brainless zombies shambling towards a unified goal. If you’ve ever seen any of these and thought the concept was pretty cool, Shamblerot Vectorum may be for you. It's currently the strongest way to run Death Guard, for some very funny (and frustrating) reasons.

Changelog

  • 10-21-2026: Updated for 11th edition
  • 4-26-2026 (Initial Publication)

Detachment Cost: 2 DP

Disposition: Disruption

The Detachment goes all in on Poxwalkers. On their own, Poxwalkers are a pretty solid unit. They’re cheap, can start at midboard, and often take more investment to remove than their cost would imply. This Detachment gives you a suite of tools to overwhelm your opponent with bodies and eventually win through attrition. The detachment rule is incredibly unique, giving you free additional units to work with, while the stratagems on offer are versatile and powerful - Shambling Wall is one of the game's most frustrating effects, and can create some devastating results on the table when opponents aren't prepared for it.

Detachment Rule: Numberless Horde

In your Command phase, in each of the specified battle rounds, you add a 10-model unit of Poxwalkers to your army, placed into Strategic Reserves. The rounds you do this on depends on the game size - 2 and 3 for Incursion, 2, 3, and 4 for Strike Force, and 2 through 5 for Onslaught.

Additionally, Poxwalkers units in your army gain the BATTLELINE keyword.

This is unique as a Detachment rule, and it lets you run nine units of Poxwalkers. That's insane, and while you may not actually run that many, chances are good you're going to run at least 30 to 40 Poxwalkers in your base army, then add three more units of ten during a game.

Poxwalkers already boast a very solid statline, with T4, a 5+ feel no pain, OC1 and LETHAL HITS on their weapons. They're effective speed bumps - particularly against infantry units, where they're liable to get back some dead models when they swing back - and act as potent plague spreaders for your army. The true value of Poxwalkers is being vectors for your contagion auras, delivering that incredibly important -1 to saves for Rattlejoint Ague. They aren't powerhouses even with 20 model units, but what they do bring to the table is the ability to take up space, project auras, protect your units, and cling to life with 1-2 models remaining in ways which are guaranteed to frustrate your opponent.

One key change with the 10th edition Codex was allowing the Noxious Blightbringer and the Malignant Plaguecaster to attach to units of Poxwalkers. The Blightbringer does a lot to help them zoom up the table and the Plaguecaster helps push them toward being a more consistent threat (although still not a particularly potent one). Typhus can also join a unit of Poxwalkers, and his Eater Plague ability can return models to the unit, making him a very strong include in this Detachment. However, if you attach any of these models to the unit, the unit will lose its Infiltrate ability, which means you’re either coming from reserves or footslogging through the table or riding in a transport. That's not nearly as big a deal in 11th edition, where Infiltrating is worse than it used to be.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

All of these enhancements only work while the models bearing them are leading Poxwalker units, so they’ll be going on Plaguecasters and Blightbringers. It's worth noting you can combine some of these effects by attaching two characters to the same unit.

  • Witherbone Pipes (25 points) – This one can only go on a Noxious Blightbringer. Poxwalkers in his unit get +1 OC and +1 to leadership/battle shock tests. 2 OC Poxwalkers can be incredibly annoying and make for a great brick to sit on an objective, and the +1 Leadership is helpful for avoiding Ld 8+ failures. That said, you're going to use your 20man Poxwalker unit as ablative wounds for a Defiler, so this isn't really what you want.
  • Lord of the Walking Pox (15 points) – Lets the bearer's unit come in from strategic reserves at any time as if it's the third battle round. This lets you apply some serious pressure early and forces your opponent to screen their deployment zone well or sets you up for a gnarly turn one charge. That said, you aren't trying to bring in units of Poxwalkers from Strategic Reserves eary game anyqs.
  • Sorrowsyphon (10 points) – This one gives a Plaguecaster +1 damage to his Plague Wind weapon at the cost of d3 Poxwalkers every time he shoots. This isn't optional, but it's pretty good, as doing D3+1 damage is really good. That said, this won't apply to the weapon being shot from a Transport, so just keep that in mind.
  • Talisman of Burgeoning (25 points) – Gives the Poxwalkers in the bearer's unit +1 toughness. Really simple, but T5 Poxwalkers are super annoying to remove. More important now that bolters and marine base strength 5, and something you want on a unit of 20 models if you're taking it, just to maximize value. But again, the problem is that your 20man brick isn't meant to be tough, it's meant to be a bunch of ablative wounds for other units. 
Poxwalkers by Craig "MasterSlowPoke" Sniffen

Stratagems

As you might expect, your Stratagems primarily benefit Poxwalkers. They're all priced to move at 1 CP.

  • Grip of the Walking Pox (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in the Fight phase, when an enemy unit targets one of your Poxalkers units. After that unit fights, roll a D6 for every poxwalker that died from an enemy attack; on a 6 you do a mortal to the enemy unit and if those mortals kill anything you can return models to the unit. This is a neat threat and could theoretically make attaching your unit a chore, but the reality is that you aren't likely to get a ton of models back this way - if you lose 18 models, on average you'll do three mortal wounds, and that may mean getting one model back. It certainly be swingy, but the juice isn't worth the squeeze here most of the time. 
  • Smeared With Filth (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in the Fight phase. Pick a Poxwalkers unit that died this phase, and an enemy unit that made attacks which targeted it this phase. That enemy unit is afflicted until the end of the game. This is pretty handy for punishing opponents who charge into your Infiltrator screens - your Poxwalkers' primary objective being that close is mostly just to put the opponent in contagion range and block their movement early, so if you can force them to charge you and then still keep them in contagion after, that's pretty much mission accomplished.
  • Gnawing Hunger (Battle Tactic, 1 CP) – Used in your Command phase. You select a unit of Poxwalkers and they get +1 move, strength, and attacks until the end of the turn. This makes them movement 7” with a blightbringer and can really help them close distances and clog up the table. The extra Strength and Attack put them at S4 with 3 attacks each which isn't amazing, but with Lethal Hits and the -1 to saves from Rattlejoint Ague means they can punch up more effectively than people realize. Good in a pinch, but the movement bonus here is the real winner.
  • Hidden Amongst the Dead (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – This can only be used on a Poxwalker unit without an attached character. Used in the movement phase to give a unit of Poxwalkers held in reserve the DEEP STRIKE ability. Unfortunately this can’t be comboed with Lord of the Walking Pox but this is still really solid for getting your spare Poxwalkers where they need to be for actions or to capture objectives which are otherwise 
  • Shock and Horror (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – This one works on any Death Guard unit. Used in the charge phase just after you finish a Charge move on a Death Guard unit. Every unit within Engagement range of your unit must take a Battleshock test at -1. This can be really nasty in a pinch, especially if you can combine it with the extra -1 from a sigil on a unit of Plague Marines or Deathshroud Terminators. It's not necessarily reliable, but if you can get off charges against multiple units it can turn of Stratagems and stop your opponent from scoring key objectives. It's worth it to throw this out when you can directly cost your opponent VP with it.
  • Shambling Wall (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Pick a Death Guard unit that was just targeted by a shooting attack and one friendly Poxwalkers unit within 3" that is visible to the attacking unit. Until the end of the phase, every time your unit is targeted by an attack, if the poxwalkers unit you picked is visible to the attacking model and an eligible target to attack, then instead of allocating that attack to your unit, you don't make a saving throw and instead you kill a number of Poxwalkers in your unit equal to the damage characteristic of that attack. This is amazing for something like Mortarion or a Defiler to deter enemy attacks and keeping him in the game, and great if you have a lot of damage 1 shots you want to shrug off. Note that your poxwalkers have to be visible for this, so make sure they aren't HIDDEN to the attacking unit.

This last one needs an extra addendum because it has some proper bullshit associated with it. As of this writing, according to how the rules for wound allocation work in the attack sequence in 11th edition, this is busted. That's because save rolls happen before damage allocation now, so when you shoot a unit like a Defiler or Mortarion with this, the sequence will be:

  1. Opponent rolls hit rolls
  2. Opponent rolls wound rolls
  3. You roll saves
  4. You allocate damage to models based on the allocation group, starting with the lowest rolls and going to the highest

WHAT THIS MEANS: If you take say, 18 wounds on your Defiler from AP-1, 1-damage shots while it's standing within 3" of a visible unit of ten Poxwalkers. You'd then roll 18 saves. Then you immediately pick up ten Poxwalkers, "using up" the ten worst saves in the batch. If all of the remaining 8 rolls were a 4+, then you'd count 8 successful saves and walk away with no damage taken.

This is, frankly, bonkers. It's technically correct, but definitely taking advantage of a loophole in the 11th edition rules where the new way saves and damage are allocated don't mix with the way the Stratagem was written.

NOTE: YOU DON'T HAVE TO LIVE THIS WAY. You are, of course, welcome to play it more sensibly, or if you're running an event, rule it in such a way that the original intent - no saves are rolled - is preserved. But if you're playing against this and it comes up, note that the "correct" interpretation is the far stronger one.

Poxwalkers. Credit: Rockfish

Playing This Detachment

One key value here is that this is a 2 DP Detachment, freeing you up to pair it with Paragons of Putrescence or Flyblown Host. Which is good, because you'll need to get a better Disposition. The usual pick here is Paragons, because that will get you Priority Assets, a disposition that works very well conceptually with having tons of cheap Poxwalker bodies to play with. One thing Paragons gets you is the Rejuvenating Swarm Enhancement, which can go on a Plaguecaster or Blightbringer and be used to give a 20-model blob of Poxwalkers -1 to be wounded by attacks with a Strength higher than their Toughness. That's a much stronger buff than +1 Toughness, and you can combine the Blightbringer with Typhus on a big unit of Poxwalkers to get the most value out of their buffs and Typhus' ability to bring back dead models with his psychic attack. That unit also gets +3" to its contagion range from having a character.

Outside of the strategy of “bring a lot of Poxwalkers” you’re looking to control the table and continually apply pressure to your opponent throughout the game and win by attrition. Even with buffs, Poxwalkers aren’t exactly offensive powerhouses, so don’t expect to remove units with even a 20 block of them. Instead your primary focus here is using Poxwalkers to perform actions for your primary, block enemy movement, and spread contagion for your big threats. You want to put a 10-model block near your big threats (Mortarion, Defiler) to soak up damage and keep them around.

In that regard, Shamblerot armies love Defilers and Mortarion, as being able to eat a bunch of wounds intended for your big targets makes removing them all that much harder. Opponents already have to gamble on whether it's worth it to throw mass resources at these units; knowing they'll be wasting their first ten damage even trying - only to watch that unit get replaced, free of charge - can be downright demoralizing.

If you're taking Paragons, the character-focused Stratagems give you a lot of value out of taking attached units. Territorial Infection is insanely good on a unit of 20 Poxwalkers, giving them +1 OC for your turn at the start of the Command phase, while the extra 3" of Contagion range makes for Poxwalker units which can cause more problems without getting too close. And Aggravus Spasms can be used to "out" enemy units near your character-led poxwalkers, upping their Detection range by 6" for units further away to shoot.

Strengths

  • The Most Unique Detachment Rule in the Game. Nothing else in the game works like this detachment does. Getting a total of 9 of the same unit is something no other army in the game can do and it's a very strong ability even if it's just Poxwalkers.
  • Incredibly Frustrating Board Control. With Poxwalkers gaining Infiltrate, you can feasibly have 60 bodies in midboard at the start of the game while only dedicating about 400 points to the effort. If you’re going first, your opponent is gonna end up in Pox jail pretty quick.
  • Durability. Protecting your biggest threats with Poxwalkers can make them maddeningly difficult to kill, especially when your opponent has to wound against T11 and T12 to even push through.

Weaknesses

  • The Hobby Commitment. While not a mechanical weakness, you are gonna have to paint 100 Poxwalkers (and that's on the low end) to make this Detachment really sing. The models aren’t as simple to paint up as Termagants so this is gonna take a significant amount of time to get battle ready.
  • Blast and Cleave. Blast and Cleave weapons are gonna rip right through your hordes and they’ll generally be on platforms your hordes aren’t equipped to deal with.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

A Sample List

There's no getting around the Poxwalker commitment you're going to need to play this Detachment. That said, the big threats are also key here. This teams-focused list from Innes Wilson gives a good view of how this kind of list plays in a competitive environment. Innes took this list to a 5-0 finish at the Scottish Open Team Championship and it's very similar to other successful lists we've seen. The big difference is using a battle cannon Knight instead of a second Defiler.

Your three big threats here are Mortarion, the Defiler, and the double Battle Cannon Despoiler. You can protect the prior two with Poxwalkers, while the Knight is just here to take advantage of Rattlejoint Ague and the extra AP push. The double-attached 20-model unit of Poxwalkers here features Typhus and a Noxious Blightbrlinger with Rejuvenating Swarm, which gives the list an annoyingly difficult to kill swarm of T4 goobers to sit at midtable. The other unit features a plaguecaster and that unit and the solo Plaguecaster go in the Rhino to create the "party bus" with two plaguecasters shooting out of the top. The third Poxwalkers unit is there to protect Mortarion or the Defiler, and so will new units added to the army.

Final Thoughts

And that's a wrap for our beloved brain-dead bozos. This Detachment is really neat, giving you extra units throughout the game gives you a great lever for applying continuous pressure. Beyond that, it's also very strong. There’s a lot of great support here and a lot to like. Poxwalkers are already one of the best units in the book and this gives you another way to play them with a very unique playstyle.

title: BattleTech Mech Overview: Avatar
content:
Howdy and welcome back to Mech Overview! This week we are taking a look at one of, in the humble opinion of one of the two wolves inside of me, the most underrated mechs in BattleTech. The Avatar has a lot of things working against it. It's ugly as sin, it is an omni-mech with fixed equipment, it has an IS XL engine. But through all of that, one thing reigns supreme, and makes the Avatar one of the game's best units.

Cost.

Avatar. Credit: Rockfish

The Avatar is a huge beneficiary of BV, with nearly all variants coming in at screamingly low prices for their capabilities. It isn't flashy, it's ugly, its a gangly freak, but when it comes to raw, unfiltered efficiency, few things can compete with it. It is the perfect list filler, and its variants can fit any role you could possibly need a mech to fill while doing it cheaper than most of your other options. This price makes it a tournament staple, as does its wide availability. The sheer breadth of situations that the Avatar configs can cover is nearly unmatched by any other omni-mech, particularly for the price.

So, without further yapping, let's get into it!

Chassis

As mentioned above, the Avatar is an omni-mech, meaning that all variants share the same frame at the core. The Avatar weighs in at 70 tons, moves 4/6, carries 10 double heat sinks, a reasonable (if not incredible) armor load, nearly maxed out everywhere but the limbs. While I would love to see a bit more armor on the arms, as they fall under the threshold for an AC/20, biasing armor towards the torso is usually the optimal choice, particularly because the Avatar also uses an IS XL engine, meaning it would die if it lost one of those side torsos.

The Avatar has a few other pieces of hard mounted equipment, with CASE in both side torsos and a pair of hard mounted medium lasers in the center torso. Normally fixed equipment like this is a substantial downside, but very nearly every possible config you could think of, aside from a pure energy boat, is happy to have all of this equipment. The medium lasers ensure that no matter what an Avatar config will always have bare-minimum viable backup weapons, and the CASE, as of the Core Rulebook, means that the Avatar will very often survive an ammo explosion in one of those side torsos.

In addition, even with all that hard mounted equipment, the Avatar still manages to fit an impressive 34 tons of pod space for weaponry. With the mech not having any crit-eating structural components such as Endo-Steel or Ferro Fibrous, it also has a pretty impressive amount of crit space to spend. The possibilities are limitless, and while the Avatar is somewhat held back from filling literally every role by its slow speed, there is functionally no config you can conceive of that wouldn't fit in one.

Speaking of Configs, let's get talking about those.

Variants

These mechs have all been reviewed based on a standard F through S scale, which you can find described on our landing page here (along with all of our other ‘Mech reviews, the name of the box you can buy to get any of the mechs we have covered, and our general methodology).

O

The "prime" config, to borrow Clan terms, is designed as a trooper, capable of filling nearly any role. For an exceptionally reasonable 1395 BV you get an LB-10X autocannon, 2 medium pulse lasers, a pair of machine guns, and two LRM-10s with Artemis. This is a phenomenal Swiss army knife of a mech, and is one of my most frequently used configs. Damage at all ranges is decent if not incredible, with the medium lasers, autocannon, and pulse lasers giving a bit of short range bite to a mech that is equally happy to hold its distance and chip in damage.

This flexibility gives the O a huge amount of value. In a tournament or mission setting with objectives, it is equally effective pushing forwards to brawl with your frontline as it is hanging back to secure an objective against enemy attacks. It won't be the star of your list, it isn't a world beater, but it is effective, efficient, and reliable. There are better mechs at anything it does, but there aren't many other mechs in this price range that are as adept at solving as many problems at once as the Avatar O.

My Rating: B+. Shockingly effective, extremely efficient. Never bad and always worth taking, but rarely top of the game.

Mercenary Avatar. Credit: Jack Hunter

OA

The OA is a different animal, but it is no less effective. Instead of a generalist, the OA is a close range specialist, and a fairly effective one. For one, it carries 4 jump jets. 4/6/4 isn't a terribly impressive movement profile, but it can help with clearing terrain on the way in. Its weaponry is very focused, with an AC/20, two SRM-6s, and the fixed medium lasers providing its main firepower. It does carry an ER large laser as an afterthought, ensuring it isn't totally helpless while it closes in, but it really does need to close in.

Core Rules are extremely kind to the OA. It carries sufficient AC/20 ammo to load a mix of precision and AP in your preferred ratio while still getting through a game, and two tons of SRM ammo allows for your preferred mix of acid, inferno, and standard SRMs. With AP ammo and acid SRMs, the Avatar OA can do horrifying things to the Hammerheads, Viking IICs, Savage Wolfs, and other weird armor nightmare engines that have started cropping up more and more lately.

At 1481 BV the OA is a substantial upgrade over something like a Victor 9B, filling the same role to a significantly higher level of effectiveness. It is somewhat fragile and needs to be deployed carefully, but in the right situation a well applied OA can swing a game hard if used right.

My Rating: B+. Trades flexibility for substantial power in its niche. Priority target if you see one across the table from you.

OB

In a near-exact reversal of the OA, the OB is a pure long range specialist. With paired LRM-15s and paired LRM-10s, all with Artemis IV, it is a very effective fire support mech for its 1496 BV cost. While it is very vulnerable up close, with only the fixed medium lasers, the OB is extremely happy to sit in your second line, holding an objective or a good firing position and slinging quite a bit of damage down range. Not incredible, not terrible, overall an effective mech for its purpose. If you need IS LRMs on a budget, this is a good choice.

My Rating: B. Less impressive in its niche than other Avatars, but still effective for cost. Mostly held back by IS LRMs being finnicky and difficult to use.

OC

A remix on the O, the OC is more of a fire support mech than a generalist. For 1406 BV you get a PPC, an Ultra AC/5, two LRM-10s, and a C3 master. Firepower here is decent and cheap, though it is vulnerable to enemy mechs closing into its minimum range and exploiting the weak backup weaponry. As a C3 master it is well designed to hang back at long range and not get in danger, but even outside of a C3 list this could see use in a similar fashion to the OB. It trades the Artemis and some of the max damage of the OB for a bigger hit in the PPC, while being a fair chunk cheaper. Decent, not incredible, and outshined by other Avatars.

My Rating: C+. Adequate but unimpressive, improved in a C3 list but C3 remains bad even with new Core.

OD

The Overdose here is in vicious competition with the OR for the title of "Most Improved Avatar" with the Core Rulebook. Weaponry consists of paired MRM-20s, a pair of ER medium lasers, a light gauss rifle, and the fixed medium lasers. This is a pretty scary close ranged loadout with a decent long ranged gun, but much like the OA this is a mech that wants to be closing in, not hanging back. With a decent firing profile of everything but an ER medium lasers up close, you get good damage for a low price, coming in at 1475 BV. The OA is flashier and scarier, but the OD is still a close ranged powerhouse if applied correctly.

Oh, it also has a C3 slave, and MRM mechs really do love being in a C3 network. I still wouldn't recommend C3, but if you are going to be using it, the OD is a perfectly good mech to put in a network.

My Rating: B. Good damage up close, but lacking the knockdown power of an OA.

OE

The OE is, in many ways, an upgraded OC. Weaponry consists of an ER PPC, an ER medium laser, an and Ultra AC/10. Combined with the fixed medium lasers, this is a pretty solid amount of firepower at any range. It also carries a C3i system and an ECM suite. The ECM is very helpful for shutting down enemy Artemis and NARC and will see use in most games as a result. C3i is still not great, but it is better than regular C3 in a lot of ways.

Overall another solid all-range trooper, but it is more expensive than many Avatars at 1563 BV. For the price, I would often just take an O, but I could see the argument for an OE.

My Rating: B. Solid and useful at all ranges.

OF

A bit of a hybrid, the OF mixes traits of the OE and OA. It carries an ER PPC and an LB-20X, along with the fixed medium lasers. In addition, it has the same 4 jump jets as the OA, and can broadly be used in the exact same way. While missing the SRMs does sting, the LB-20 is an interesting side-grade, exchanging ammo flexibility for better range and the cluster shot. LB-20 cluster shot can be game winning in the right circumstance, so I see the two weapons as roughly equivalent.

The only real issue is the cost. At 1667 BV, the OF is substantially more expensive than an OA for a mech that is for the most part a side grade rather than a true upgrade. If you need the cluster shot, or you would prefer a better long-ranged closing gun, I can see an argument for the OF, but in my opinion it is broadly less efficient.

My Rating: B-. Solid, but let down by cost.

OG

The OG is dead simple. Two Gauss Rifles, two medium lasers, nothing else. For 1775 BV this is one of the games absolute cheapest double gauss mechs, and unlike a Jagermech DG or Sun Cobra it has real armor to keep those guns safe.

This is a shockingly boring, extremely focused mech. It is one of the very best mechs in all of BattleTech at doing what it does, with its only real competitor at this price point being.... The Avatar OH.

My Rating: A, there is no better way to get two gauss rifles on the cheap.

OH

The OH then is probably even better. For 1604 BV you get two Heavy PPCs, two MML-3s with Artemis, and the paired medium lasers. This is one of the games cheapest double headcapper mechs, and the backup weapons are perfectly adequate if unimpressive. You take this to sling HPPCs at people, and it does that very, very cheaply. If you have never used a dirt cheap HPPC mech, you should give it a try, they nearly always trade up and the OH is probably the absolute best of them. A Flashman 9M can do the job better, but at 300 more BV, it is substantially more expensive and doesn't fit in a list nearly as easily.

My Rating: A+, best in class for price for this role. Can and will win games on its own.

OI

The OI is fairly simple, and is yet another cheap double headchopper Avatar. For 1606 BV you get two Thunderbolt 15s, two ER medium lasers, and the fixed lasers. This is also good, though Thunderbolts are much more finnicky to use than gauss rifles or HPPCs. If you can indirect fire it it will be better, it will be marginally worse at direct fire, but 15 damage per gun is 15 damage per gun. You are spoiled for choice with double headchopper Avatars, and all of them are good.

My Rating: A-, solid double headchopper for a low cost. Let down by Thunderbolts being annoying to use.

ComGuards Avatar. Credit: Lynn B.

OR

The other competitor for "Most Improved Avatar", the OR is a mix-tech mech with a huge amount going for it. At 1833 it is a bit pricey for an Avatar, but the weapon load is very much worth it. It carries a Clan gauss rifle, a Clan ER large laser, a Clan streak SRM-4, and an MRM-40, in addition to the fixed lasers. With a simple firing pattern where you fire either the ER large or the MRM, the OR does good damage at long range which ramps up to fantastic damage up close. While it is approaching a bit too expensive, this is a solid mech with a lot going for it. Use it similarly to the OD and it will serve you well.

My Rating: A-. Solid and can spike some insanely high damage, but you are paying for it.

OU

This is a C3 mech with two LRT-15s and two SRT-4s. Its an underwater mech, and while water is semi-playable in new core, it is still basically worthless in nearly all games.

My Rating: N/A, go fish.

OJ

The Orange Juice is the most expensive Avatar at 2223, and acts as an upgraded OG. It carries a pair of HAG/30s along with the fixed medium lasers. This is a lot of damage at a great range, HAGs are pretty incredible if you have never used them. While I can't recommend it over other Avatars due to the BV and the relative fragility, it is deeply hilarious and I have had some very fun games with it in the past.

My Rating: C. Hilarious, swingy, and expensive. Worth using if you have spare BV, but prioritize other aspects of your list first.

OBLO

And finally, sitting in a weird semi-special category, the OBLO is almost exactly the same as the OE. For 1550 BV it trades the ER medium laser and UAC/10 out for an LB10 and 4 jump jets, it is otherwise identical. This is fine, its an adequate mech, I rate it slightly below the OE but it is fine if you want the LB more than the UAC.

My Rating: C+. Fine, but the damage is somewhat low.

Conclusion

There really isn't a single bad Avatar. Its a solidly playable mech in all configs, and some of its configs are extremely good at what they do for the price. You will literally never regret including an Avatar in your list, and you can always find one to plug a hole or fix a problem your list is having. I love the Avatar and I always have, it just works. It isn't fancy, its ugly, it can be boring, but it works all the time in a way that most other mechs can really struggle to. A real Omni-Mech, a Swiss army knife for every possible situation and every possible role you could want a 4/6 heavy mech to fill. Use more Avatars, I command thee.

title: MTG Star Trek breaks one of Magic's most infamous combos
content:
Oh good, MTG players found a way to break Food Chain! This classic combo seen in Legacy and cEDH decks is about to get even stronger, thanks to a brand new card from the Star Trek set. That card features Khan, one of the franchise's most iconic villains.

Khan, Wrathful Heart is a legendary creature that can be cast from exile, which immediately makes it an obvious choice for Food Chain decks. For those unfamiliar, this combo relies on Food Chain, alongside any creature that can be cast from exile - such as Misthollow Griffin or Squee. You keep on sacrificing those creatures to Food Chain and recasting them, with a net gain of one mana each time, allowing you to make infinite mana with which to win the game.

What makes Khan, Wrathful Heart so much better than these older options is that he has another effect. He can also turn creatures or artifacts into card draw. Traditionally, for a Food Chain cEDH deck, you've needed to run a commander that provides immediate value from entering the battlefield (be that card draw or direct damage) so you can keep casting and exiling it with your unlimited mana and have a built in way to win.

Pantlaza or Atraxa, cards that fetch up other cards on ETB, are classic examples of Food Chain commanders in this vein.

Khan provides that value all by himself, though, which means technically any deck can now be a Food Chain deck. You can't actually whiff as long as your commander is a creature, since you can sacrifice them to Khan if you don't draw anything you want to put in the bin. Remember you have infinite mana in this scenario; commander tax may as well not exist.

I'm excited to see what black-based Food Chain decks crop up around Khan, and if this widens the pool of commanders folks are using for this archetype.

Share your own deck lists and join likeminded tabletop fans over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: Tabletop Battles' Eldfall Chronicles Northern Wind Campaign Report, Part I
content:
On the frost-armored slopes of Mt. Byodo, evil stirs.

The Empire of Soga is well aware of the curse that afflicts Mt. Byodo. Two hundred years ago, that curse boiled out of the mountains, slaying the lucky and carrying off the rest for unspeakable cannibal rites in their frozen fastness.  The Empire named these monsters Oni and raised up a caste of specialized soldiers, the Onitaoshi, to hunt them and slay them. Some years the Oni threat waxed strong, others it seemed to slumber, but it never went away entirely. The Oni come with the winter and retreat before the encroaching spring, but like the fierce blizzards that blow down from Mt. Byodo, they always return.

The Kitano clan, the grim-faced wardens of the Empire's northern provinces, report that the Oni are on the move again.  Villages are found sacked and abandoned, isolated monasteries burned. Worst of all, the Nine-Tailed Empress, the Grand Priestess of the Soga Empire, has had a vision: a red moon rising above a holy mountain, its peak split by some unimaginable violence.

The Empire did not have long to wonder at the meaning of that portent. One night, with a shattering crash that was heard for miles around, the peak of Mt. Byodo tore open and spilled forth a torrent of foulness. The Oni have returned, but this time, they bring with them fresh horrors: the unquiet dead pouring out of newly opened tombs, monsters that defy description, and worse things yet. There is a presence at the top of Mt. Byodo now. A rift has been torn open, bleeding profane magic into the world.

The people of Soga - and all the people of Calad - know what such a thing means. Rifts like that one brought the downfall of the Elder Age and sundered the world. It is long past time that the Oni of Mt. Byodo, and whatever force drives them onward, are dealt with once and for all. Clan Kitano Onitaoshi, monster hunters of the Imperial Keshobarai, and foreign mercenaries and would-be heroes alike, all gather in the north. Will you join the call?

Northern Wind

Northern Wind is the first major expansion for Freecompany's Eldfall Chronicles.  In addition to adding models to the skirmish game, Northern Wind is itself a campaign board game, tracking the progress of a group of heroes seeking to end the Oni threat. We've previously reviewed the models and the game itself - this is the first in a series of campaign reports, as Sam and Jake brave the elements and the Oni in hopes of gold, glory, and a good tale to impress hunky stableboys and/or winsome barmaids.

While Northern Wind does allow some hero customization, we'll be playing with the base party:

Credit: Freecompany

Seigen, of the Keshobarai, an exiled and disgraced noble (framed for a crime he didn't commit, natch). He's the only one with more than one wound and he has more armor than the rest of the party put together, but luckily he can take hits for his friends. He's not Mr. Personality but at least you know what you're getting with him.

Credit: Freecompany

Tharos, the One-Eyed Wolf, a totally cool dark elf who grew up as an orphan, was betrayed and left for dead, wears a half-face mask, has a magic hawk, etc. He is basically a dark romantasy character except he doesn't canonically hate women. Obviously this is your ranged damage dealer.

Credit: Freecompany

Anari, Erudite Prodigy, a skilled mage whose mixed ancestry limited her ability to advance within the elegant, scholarly, and extremely racist society of the Helian League. Despite being discriminated against, she's a brilliant sorceress. If this were a romantasy series she would have a will-they-or-won't-they thing with both Seigen and Tharos, but the Anari/Tharos tag on Ao3 would be three times larger. She's your spellslinger.

Credit: Freecompany

Na'ra, Veil Watcher, a catgirl Mau (wait, really?) from the Sand Kingdoms. Since the role of "stealth assassin" is already taken, she's a necromancer, I guess? She has a tragic backstory that involves the word "younglings." She's fast and strong, she's armed with claws that can't be broken or lost, and her magic is really good at buffing herself and others.

The campaign opens with a few pages of fiction where the four PCs' players introduce themselves to each other at a Standard Issue Fantasy Tavern (Samurai Flavor), along with DMPC Asano, a wise commander who walks around wearing an I WILL DIE OR TURN EVIL sandwich board. After the requisite wisecracking and a little drinking, they all go to sleep, whereupon a huge horde of Oni arrive and sack the camp.

That leads directly into the first mission, which is basically a tutorial. The PCs have lost almost all of their gear and spellcasting is blocked; the camp is overrun by Oni, although it's easy enough to sneak past them (and sneak you will; fighting Oni is a dicey gambit at the best of times, let alone when you're stripped of your mojo and weapons). You can potentially find and free Asano, but beyond that this mission is just about teaching you how movement and activations work and letting you scrounge up some random shortswords, daggers and whatnot.

Our heroes escape the burning camp and, of course, shortly arrive at a fork in the road. Anari notes that the Oni have put up a barrier that blocks the use of non-Oni magic; this will need to come down if they are to have any chance at survival, let alone success.  Meanwhile, Seigen points out that they are armed with little more than steak knives and harsh language, and that recovering their weapons should be a priority.

Naturally, the party - outnumbered and outgunned in a hostile wilderness full of gigantic demons, and stripped of their magical powers - sticks together, first gathering weapons and then cooperating to take down the anti-magic barrier.

Just kidding!  They split up.  The menfolk go scavenging for sharp objects while the women are put in charge of unraveling a massive enchantment without the benefit of their own powers.  Just as the Elders intended.

Mission 2: On the Oni Trail

Quest Log entry for the Northern Wind mission On the Oni Trail.

Sam's Game

Freed from the tyranny of female companionship, Seigen and Tharos make their way onward, farting, scratching their balls, and pointing out particularly suggestive looking trees and rocks. Mission 2 finds our heroes on a long, narrow trail, leading towards a partially collapsed shelter. There's an Oni on the path ahead, but luckily he is looking away and badly hurt - and even more luckily, he's stooped under the weight of lucre.

Oni Marauders are terrifying foes, but this one has just one wound remaining and two Weak Points on him, in addition to being Distracted. Weak Points are applied whenever an attack hits but fails to wound its target (either because of a Dodge roll or just failing to crack armor). You can cash in a number of Weak Points equal to the tier of an enemy to turn any one attack roll into a critical hit (that is, a hit that bypasses armor). In addition, if the enemy is adjacent to an open edge, you can just shove them off the map for an instant kill (although doing so costs you any loot they might be carrying). Oni Marauders are Tier 3, so hitting this one just once, even if you don't penetrate his armor and instantly kill him, will set him up for a crit.

In this mission, the Oni goes first, but as he is Distracted he doesn't follow the ordinary "Hostile Behavior" card that dictates his actions. Instead, he simply ambles towards the exit, whistling a jaunty tune. Our heroes sneak up behind him and cut his throat without much trouble; as he has spent all of his AP walking towards the exit, he cannot React and smush a hero to paste with his huge club. Tharos pauses to loot the body and uncovers some medicine (helpful, as it allows an Incapacitated hero to heal themselves without needing help), another dagger, and his Thenian Crossbow. "Melissa!" he cries, caressing the crossbow with entirely too much affection.

Seigen does not have time to be weirded out by this display, however, as rounding the corner he sees another Oni up ahead. This one is also freighted with goodies, and is slightly less wounded than his companion. "He's making for the exit!"

"Not if I have anything to say about it," Tharos replies. Ignoring his companion's rolling eyes, Tharos sights down the length of his crossbow and fires. The bolt misses the Oni entirely and crashes into a worm-eaten wooden pillar holding up an ancient gate. The pillar, already weakened by time and neglect, crumbles, and the entire gate collapses just as the Oni passes underneath; the heavy beams inflict another Wound and another Weak Point on him, leaving him with just one Wound remaining and two Weak Points applied.

"Uh... all according to keikaku," Tharos says. "Translator's note: keikaku-"

Seigen is not listening to his companion's trivialities. He charges forward, shortsword in hand, screaming the battle cry of his clan. The Oni, distracted, does not hear him until the last minute; it does not have time to bring its club free before he smites its head from its shoulders. The beast collapses, spilling the treasure it was carrying: a smoke bomb and a massive polearm.

"Stonesplitter!" Seigen says, satisfaction evident in his voice. He sheaths the shortsword and hefts the polearm, trying a few experimental cuts.

"So it's ok when he names his weapon," Tharos grumbles. But nobody is listening. With their tools of the trade recovered, the men prepare to meet up at the Hilltop Temple.

Jake's Game

Join me in a short intermission from Sam's lovely narrative summaries while I dig into the gameplay of my time running the same mission. Personally, I look at the narrative and fluff from games as a nice garnish but the main draw has always been the mechanics. Plus there's no way I can top what you just read so I won't even try!

Like Sam, I had investigated the optional intrigue token in the previous mission which meant my heroes found and rescued Asano. As a result, the party picked up their first Fate Token. There are three colors of fate tokens in Northern Wind, each with a letter of the alphabet on them. In this case, I got a purple A which means... something. The Quest Log uses these Fate Tokens as a way of tracking which outcomes you have in missions, so I assume at some point the fact that we rescued Asano will be relevant and change how something plays out.

Seigen and Tharos came into this mission with a basic shortsword, dagger, and hatchet between them. Since part of the setup for this mission involved making a loot deck with some really juicy weapon upgrades, I knew what the potential rewards were. I definitely wanted to take out the Oni Marauders here to secure both Stonesplitter and, uh, Melissa.

So, Seigen and Tharos promptly approached the first distracted and mostly dead Oni Marauder. Easy pickings. I then proceeded to miss three of their four attacks, not only failing to injure the Marauder but also failing to even inflict an additional weak point on it. Seigen's final attack hit... but failed to wound. That left me out of activations, made the Oni aware of my heroes' presence, and meant next turn was going to probably be pretty painful.

Fortunately, the action/reaction mechanics of the game meant that when the Oni went to smack Seigen, I could choose to attack back. This triggers a confrontation roll where both sides are rolling to hit which simulates the back-and-forth nature of a combat complete with parries, blocks, counter-attacks, and the like. The goal is to roll under whatever your target number is (standard fare for Eldfall Chronicles) while also rolling higher than your opponent's rolls. Each side's highest roll that's still a success will negate their opponent's lower rolls. It's kind of a mouthful to explain, but feels super intuitive once you roll the dice. Combined with the action and reaction system, it makes for a dynamic and interactive set of turns regardless of which side is "up" at the time.

As the attacker, the Oni here would normally be rolling 2d20 and would succeed on any rolls equal to its OFF of 14 or less. Seigen has an ability that I chose to use which reduced the Oni down to a single die. Meanwhile, the Soga hero was swinging back with his own 1d20 roll that also succeeds on a 14 or less, matching his DEF stat. I wasn't particularly worried about this fight, though, because the Oni now had three weakpoints applied which meant I could instantly turn my attack into a critical hit -- making it into an attack that automatically wins confrontations and ignore's my target's bothersome armor. This meant no matter what, Seigen's attack would land and likely punch through while leaving him safe. That is, unless the Oni rolled a 1 and got a critical hit.

Yeah, you can guess what happened. Both fighters delivered brutal hits to each other, but Seigen lived to keep going. Thank goodness he has three health.

Seigen here preemptively moved into the Oni's space before I realized that was an awful idea. I rewound that right after the picture. Credit: Jake Bennington

The remaining Oni only needed two damage to take out and I had four attacks. Easy. Tharos moved up and threw his hatchet -- miss. Okay, that's fine. Seigen advanced into the same space and attacked. Another miss. Good grief, guys. This meant I needed to get damage off of both of my final attacks before risking another Oni clap-back. Seigen swung again and hit, this time getting damage in. I elected to spend a single weakpoint token to knock the Oni back into the exit space. My Tharos finishes it off with a thrown dagger to the precarious structure and collapses it onto the Oni for the killing blow.

My versions of Seigen and Tharos, slightly more banged up than Sam's, pick through the loot to equip themselves and advance forward to meet the rest of their party later on at the Hilltop Temple.

Mission 3: Breaking the Barrier

Quest Log entry for the Northern Wind mission Breaking the Barrier.

Sam's Game

Meanwhile, Na'ra and Anari continue down the other fork. They, too, are now allowed to fart and scratch themselves, and avail themselves of the opportunity, for it will be a long, awkward mixed-gender hike to the peak of Mt. Byodo.

Following Anari's mystic senses, the two of them arrive at a winding road. Foul-smelling smoke arises from an incense burner just ahead - the source of the barrier, Anari can tell.

The goal of this mission is to purify the burners and thereby restore access to magic. This can be done by passing a Morale roll at -3, or by spending a Mana - and while Anari's morale is crap, she can convert Activation Points to Mana on a 1-to-1 basis. When the first burner is cleansed, the heroes regain the ability to cast spells of the Enchantment type (basically, buffs), with limited range; once the second one is restored, the barrier will collapse. Our heroines, armed with dagger and hatchet (and claws), edge carefully forward towards the first burner. Ephemeral spirits cluster around it, apparently drawn to its evil and stinky power.

These little guys, Vengeful Spirits, aren't that dangerous, but they are Incorporeal, meaning non-magical attacks halve their power against them. Na'ra darts forward and tries to slap the ghost silly, but her paw merely passes through, and she hisses with rage. However, the attack does inflict a Weak Point, and since Vengeful Spirits are Tier 1 enemies, one is all you need. Na'ra saves her second Activation Point, while Anari moves forward and converts an Activation Point to Mana.

The ghost tries to stab Na'ra, but aha! She's got a Reaction ready! She strikes back, making use of the Weak Point to turn her attack into a Critical Hit and thereby automatically win the Confrontation. She would still have to successfully wound the ghost - needing a 6 or less on a d20 due to its incorporeal nature - but there's an easier solution: the fighters are on the edge of the map, so she shoves the ghost like a cereal bowl left too close to the edge of the table and it plummets into the abyss, shrieking in frustration (the way I do when my cat pushes my cereal bowl off the edge of the table).

Na'ra, pleased with herself, begins purring and kneading the ground, then darts forward. Around a corner, she sees another incense burner - and more ghosts. Two of the howling spectres emerge from the driving snow. while Anari hurries forward and cleanses the burner with her Mana. The cleanse automatically applies a Weak Point to each enemy, so both of these Spirits are primed for destruction.

Magic has been partially restored! Na'ra's Artificier class allows her to cast one Enchantment on herself at the start of the round, and she picks Spectral Sight. This gives her Advantage: Undead, which translates to one free re-roll during your attack sequence per activation - so that's a reroll to hit or to wound, as needed. She tosses a throwing knife at the first spirit, and her reroll comes in clutch, dealing the one wound it takes to banish the spirit. She then darts over and slashes at the second spirit with her claws - and once again, the re-roll puts me over the top and lets me send the ghost back to hell.

Na'ra, splattered with ectoplasm, begins to lick her paws. Anari, meanwhile, freed from the burden of having to do anything taxing, waltzes past her in true High Elf fashion to take all the credit by cleansing the second burner.

With the barrier gone, our magic begins to return - but an Oni senses the loss of the barrier and turns back to block our path. Luckily, this one seems to be winded from the earlier fighting, and has three Weak Points already. He stands on the swaying rope bridge between our heroines and the exit, grinning a demonic grin.

But not for long. The yowling Na'ra darts along the bridge, fur standing on end, and swipes at him with her claws. The three Weak Points convert her attack into an automatic crit... and once again, Na'ra displays a catlike affinity for knocking things over, this time sending the surprised Oni bellowing over the edge of the rope bridge and down, down, down to a very satisfying splat far below.

"It looks like my work here is done," Anari sniffs, ignoring the fact that the kill counter now reads 4-0.  She has more important things to do.

And with that, our party reunites at the Hilltop Temple, to begin their journey in earnest...

Jake's Game

The first thing I noticed is how absolutely useless Anari is without her spellcasting abilities. She has the worst melee and ranged accuracy of the group, but she's capable of generating mana through her class ability which allows me to shut down those Profane Burners without having to roll dice. Given how cold my dice rolling has been, I leaned heavily on that. Na'ra, on the other hand, comes equipped with her special claws which are sufficient to take out these pesky ghosts. Usually.

A sample of the behavior cards included in Northern Wind. The visible side shows their active behavior while the reverse side contains all the enemy reactions. Credit: Freecompany

Just like the Oni Marauders, the Vengeful Spirits in this mission are controlled by their behavior cards. When your heroes are activating, the reactions of the enemies are dictated by a sort of flow chart. In the case of the undead, they're not quite as proactive as the Oni were. If you don't attack them and aren't standing in the same space as them, they're content to just sit there. Taking advantage of that behavior, I spent my first turn having Anari burn one of her two action points to generate a mana token and otherwise just moved up the field a bit. The Vengeful Spirit hanging out at the profane burner didn't look too intimidating, so I had Na'ra rush forward -- a move and a dodge gave her just enough movement to land in the space with the Vengeful Spirit and attack with her next action.

An attack which would have landed had the Vengeful Spirit's own retaliation not been a critical hit. The zero armor, one health Mau went down. I am not usually the kind of person to believe in bad dice, but I swapped the d20s I was using at this point.

Fortunately for our heroes, enemies do not go after incapacitated heroes. The Vengeful Spirit spent its turn (as dictated by the other side of its behavior card) moving after and attacking Anari who dodged toward her companion. Luckily, Na'ra was carrying a Medicine item from a previous mission. This item restores one health and can even be used by an incapacitated model in the Strategic phase at the start of your turn.

Credit: Jake Bennington

Na'ra eventually took out that Vengeful Spirit, Anari cleansed the first Profane Burner, and the process was repeated for the other burner once two more Vengeful Spirits joined the fray. It went a little easier this time because, as Sam mentioned, once the first burner is down your two spellcasters can finally cast a limited variety of spells. Na'ra was blessed with Burning Touch from Anari, allowing her to ignore the annoying Incorporeal rule that the ghosts had, as well as enchanting herself with Spectral Sight for re-rolls. Amusingly, Na'ra is also the only one with a heal so she was kind of my all-in-one hero for most of this mission.

That said, taking out the final burner let Anari cut loose. She had access to her full suite of Cryomancy spells which let me pelt the final Oni with Ice Spikes and finish it off with a Na'ra swipe. I didn't even consider using the bridge to shove the demon off into oblivion until I read what Sam wrote up above and now I feel a little silly.

Closing Thoughts

Jake: This is my first time playing one of these dungeon crawler campaign style games and also my first time playing any board game in a solo mode. I've found there's a bit of a learning curve to the rules for sure. They're fairly dense; I'd put it more on par with a game like D&D or 40k in terms of rules interactions and complexities than a more streamlined game like the Wrath of Ashardalon board game or Warhammer Underworlds. I followed my normal approach of reading the rulebook cover-to-cover before playing and it certainly helped, but I also had to look up quite a few things during each of the missions.

That said, having played through the first few missions, I am now feeling a lot more comfortable with the rules. So far nothing has jumped out as feeling counter-intuitive and through the process of repetition, I'm learning. Hooray.

I'd say that the only other glaring issues for me are the near overwhelming number of tokens and the time tracker which we haven't even gotten to yet. I've managed to organize the tokens into a Gamegenic Token Silo that I had sitting around and that's helped somewhat, but there are still quite a few to dig through. The time tracker doesn't feel too practical to me given that its purpose is to track the time and days remaining in the entire journey, but it's just a cardboard image with some counters you place on it. They won't stay in place in between sessions and that feels like a bit of a miss in design. Doubly so when there's also the forethought to include little envelopes that have SAVED GAME on them for you to tuck away all the heroes, their items, and their damage or weakpoints (which persist across missions). I'll probably wind up just making a basic table in Excel and printing it out so I can use a pencil to check off the days as time progresses.

The way the missions in the Quest Log are set up do an admirable job of introducing various game concepts to you. For instance, the first quest is learning the ways of moving and how both encounter and intrigue tokens work. The second introduces combat. The third adds in spellcasting. Peeking ahead, the next mission will be the first one where we utilize the chaos deck -- a deck of cards that are revealed in the enemy's turn and have various battlefield effects. This continues until we get out of the "tutorial" missions and have the full set of game mechanics in play.

I'm genuinely excited to keep playing through this campaign.

Sam: I've done games like this before, although admittedly far less complex. I like Northern Wind, and I appreciate the work that's been put in to make it feel really detailed and alive, but Jake touched on something I noticed as well: this game is lethal.  Those Oni, especially, are no joke, and there's a reason that the Marauders you fight early on come larded up with Weak Points and HP: a full-health, non-distracted Oni would pretty trivially eat our underequipped and unmagiced party alive.

Now that Tharos and Seigen have real weapons, and Anari has her spells, they stand a fighting chance, but that really highlights the issue with Na'ra: she's a melee combatant whose entire kit pushes her to engaging up close and personal, but she's incredibly fragile. Fortunately, there are a couple of alternative party members available later on, so maybe we can swap one of those in.  Sorry, neko-chan.

I'm also looking forward to the next mission. Technically, Mission 5 is the last of the "tutorial" missions, but Mission 4 is substantially more complex than everything else we've done so far, and I can see how the party is going to have to all contribute their unique skills to survive: Seigen's ironclad toughness, Anari's brilliant magic, Tharos's devastating ranged strikes, and Na'ra's ability to knock things off the high shelf.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Mechabellum
content:
When I was a kid, one of the premier Christmas presents that you could get in the pre-Nintendo era was electric football. A new one came out like every year with the previous year’s Super Bowl match up, and it was in a huge box taller than most kids. Inside was a big sheet metal football field that had a plug-in motor (I promised myself I wouldn’t call it a vibrator) on the bottom. It also came with little miniature football players - prepainted, you hobby sickos - that were mounted on these green plastic bases that had dial on them with pegs that contacted the metal field. When you turned on the motor, the players would shake and scurry all over the place and you were trying to get the one that had a tiny foam football, that you would inevitably lose, across the goal line. Those dials and pegs gave you at least some control as to whether a player would go straight, turn, or madly do donuts behind the line of scrimmage. When auto battlers started to become a thing, I kept thinking to myself, “this is really kind of like electric football.”

And this assessment holds especially true for Mechabellum, an auto battler that did some time in early access, released earlier this year, and just recently received an excellent 2.0 update that most notably adds a roguelike mode for solo players. But the meat of the game is in the online head-to-head mode where you’ll match up with another player and basically play electric football with mechs. I should also preface the remainder of this review by stating that I think this is the best auto battler I have played to date, and it is one that I keep coming back to again and again because it has an addictive quality that quite frankly makes me surprised that it is a premium title and not a free-to-play shenaniganizer despite looking and feeling like one with its dramatically over-cluttered presentation, cosmetic folderol, and a pervading sense that there is something to unlock somewhere every minute it is running. Note that there are ways to spend actual money on the game, but I do what I always do and ignore all the sales pitches.

Storyline - sure, whatever. Mechs smash into mechs. That’s all that matters. Fortunately there is much more substance in the gameplay, which can be quite compelling albeit somewhat over-complicated if you dare to dig into things like changing load outs and memorizing the rock-paper-scissors unit matchups and individual upgrade trees of the many units you can choose from. I have in fact dared, and my findings are that I actually enjoyed the game more not worrying about min-maxing minutiae or grinding for scrip.

I love the almost boardgame-like structure of the game and the good news is that you can play it quite casually so those hidden spreadsheets tracking +/- buffs and so forth don’t have to matter if you don’t want them to. When you get matched up with an opponent you choose a “character” that is really just a picture of some space soldier, a special benefit, and a couple of starter level 1 units. These can sort of form the foundation of your long-term strategy, or you might wind up going in a different direction depending on what you buy and what your opponent fields of the course of the match. There’s a setup phase before each round where you place units that can not be moved once placed for the remainder of the match, barring a special ability or function. You can also spend credits to unlock new units, buy upgrades, pay for one-shot abilities like missiles or shields, and increase your population capacity. Once both players are locked in, the battle commences, and you can practically here that vibrator, I mean motor, beneath the table running. The goal is to simply wipe out the other side down to the last mech.

The battles are awesome to watch as each side’s units automatically trundle into battle and fire missiles, lasers, and bullets into the fray. There are tanks, giant worm-like melee monsters, giant-sized fortress units, fighters, support units, robot dogs, and all kinds of mecha fun. Units have as host of specs including the expected firepower, armor, HP, speed, range and so forth so positioning your units in that setup phase is absolutely critical - if you stick a short range brawler in the backline, you might find that they aren’t as effective against an army loaded with snipers and artillery. Or, you could find that they protect your all-important energy pylons from rush attacks or 11th-hour assaults. If your pylons get taken out, your units slow down and lose some shielding, accelerating your defeat. So you’ve got to keep them safe while also pushing to take out the enemy.

The key to this working so well is that after each round you get to think on what worked or didn’t work about your setup versus what your opponent has done and then adjust for the next round, effectively building your army as you go along. If you got pounded by flyers, pick up some AA units or some flyers for yourself. If they left their left flank relatively undefended, expect that they’ll beef it up and instead pile on some pressure up the middle. I really enjoy this punch-counterpunch-counter counterpunch cadence and in fact it is the key reason I like the game so much, but I also find that it is sort of a fragile construct. Some games you just wind up on the back heel from the outset and can never really recover. I’ve also had games where I’ve been on the other end of that equation and have just completely bulldozed an opponent.

The new roguelike mode kind of exacerbates this and in a way that I don’t think is healthy. There are other solo modes that are kind of lame (training, survival mode, crappy AI bots, etc.) so this really should have been a better way to play alone than it is. The problem is that it is nine battles with four chances to fail, but each battle is against a different automated opponent with army lists pulled from actual players in the multiplayer game. So this sense of building up an army specially designed to fight your specific opponent in the specific instance of the game you are playing is lost. Although there is some flexibility in moving and selling units, it can wind up where the army you teched hard against in round 3 is very different than the one in round 4, and you wind up with an ineffective force.

Regardless, I had fun in this mode and played it more than I expected to. It does not replace the multiplayer game, and since the multiplayer game requires no communication or interaction with weirdo Mechabellumbros (they exist), it comes across as somewhat non-essential. I wish there were a little more to it, but as a sideshow to the main event it could be worse. There are also a couple of team options like a 2 vs. 2 thing and a FFA, which are great if you have a few friends looking to get into a battle but the basic head-to-head mode is what this game is really designed for.

Above it all, what I’m enjoying about this game is that it is sort of an electric football version of an RTS. It has that same feeling that you’d get sending out a giant army to crush the other giant army in Total Annihilation or Supreme Commander but without the base building, resource gathering, and terrain considerations. This makes it a fairly simple game on paper, but the decisions between rounds about what to buy and where to put it give it a great sense of depth and challenge. I’m finding that the mix of active strategic planning with passive tactical action to be an excellent option for those times when I want to play a strategy game but not get stuck in with too much process - sometimes just watching the mechs go brrrr is all you need.

Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Another big weekend is in the books, and this time it's the mighty World Eaters who are really making some noise. Terrible, gruesome noise. title: The Pokémon TCG's first 2027 release, Flowing Fists, is revealed
content:
We finally know the name of the next Pokémon TCG set coming out after Delta Reign. That set is Flowing Fists, and it's launching on February 5, 2027. We've long known that this release will focus on Mega Lucario, specifically the new version - Mega Lucario Z - which debuted in the Pokémon Legends Z-A Mega Dimension DLC last December.

Flowing Fists is the English language counterpart to Aura Seeker, the Japanese set due to launch November 27 this year. We've already seen several of its cards, including the face card Mega Lucario, and with the set roughly a month away, we should expect The Pokémon Company to release the Japanese spoilers imminently, giving the rest of us a sneak peek at what to expect in February.

Obviously, it's the full art rares we're all looking forward to seeing, but even before we knew what this set would be called, a couple of its cards had already been shown off. As mentioned, these include Mega Lucario Z, a metal type Mega ex Pokémon with an 'Aura Seeker' ability that fetches up any Supporter from your deck. It can also easily KO weak exs, as its 120 damage attack deals twice as much to them.

However, even though it only has 210 HP, Mega Lucario Z ex still can't take down the new Sigilyph ex. That's because it has an ability that blocks all damage from mega evolutions. While this only prevents damage to itself, this wall is still likely to be a meta-shaping tool, helping to keep mega evolution decks in check. Perhaps it'll be a boon to the powerful single-prize strategies that are already performing well.

Before Flowing Fists, we still have the final Pokémon set of the year, Delta Reign, to look forward to, as it launches on November 6 - just a couple of weeks away. If you haven't already, check out the chase cards from this release, from the beautiful Raikou ex to the surprisingly pretty Kecleon.
