title: The Spoiler Filled Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2 Review
content:
Hey choom! Are you curious to know what we thought about Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2? We have one that you can read that includes no spoilers at all. This one, though? This one's filled with preem spoiler content, discussion of the themes and ideas, and the authoress' thoughts on what makes Edgerunners 2 tick. So if you haven't seen it and want to not know all that, hit that back button! And if you DO wanna know all the details, well, read on. But you've been warned!

Welcome back readers to our second review of Edgerunners 2; yesterday we talked about generally why you should consider giving the show a watch and what makes it a successful sequel to the first Edgerunners, but also the ways in which it does enough unique and interesting things to be considered on its own. During that review, I tried really hard to avoid spoiling anything that wouldn't be known through trailers, the show's website, or just the first episode itself, but that also limited exactly what could be talked about or covered in greater detail.

In this second, more in-depth review, I'll be talking about the series in greater detail, working through the cast, thematics, and cinematic considerations. You can sort of consider this half review, half critical analysis of the series; if you're the type who wants to know absolutely everything about a piece of media before you give it wider consideration, or perhaps the type who, after watching it, wants a more in-depth dive, then I hope this will provide exactly that! So, let's get started, choomfie.

Man With a Movie Camera

Roman is the lead protagonist of Edgerunners 2, a 12 year old boy with dreams of making it big in Night City through the power of film. Or perhaps, in his delusion, he simply wants to prove that film is something worth watching, and he, in turn, is someone worth remembering; Cyberpunk, the series, has a heavy focus on fame, being remembered, and of making your life against the unwavering tides of ennui mean something. It was a theme in the first Edgerunners, and David Martinez's downfall, and in the 2077 game, your role as V follows similar paths.

But that isn't unique to Edgerunners, either, and perhaps with Roman, it's one of the more overt explorations of film-making as storytelling, particularly, the story of the person holding the camera. There's a long lineage of auteur theory that asks to consider the person behind the camera and the world they want to show through their film, and Roman is certainly that sort of person. The entire run of Edgerunners, up until the final arc, routinely features views of what is happening through Roman's camera, rather than his own direct point of view.

Roman's heart is fairly simple at first, wanting to make it big, wanting to get a 35mm camera, and his first target, Talia, puts him on a path that mixes him up with the revenge searching D. For a young boy like Roman, no matter his desire for fame or success, D presents as a cool, mysterious friend. An older brother type, or perhaps a dog in search of a home. Roman immediately attaches himself to D, and through filming his journey of revenge, gets himself sucked into things he likely could never comprehend.

There's a point early on when Roman watches David brutally interrogate a Maelstrom member named Helios, and the show continues swapping between Roman's camera, and then his own "direction"; as David is too forceful and violent, Roman steps in to ask questions, suggest the next scene, and help create the script of the encounter for him to film. Roman's passion for film combines with his desire to been seen, to live and tell stories through the screen. But like many creatives, Roman discovers that it's just as easy to co-opt creative energy as it is to exploit it, and as D's revenge spiral blows out of control, Roman finds himself disillusioned with helping him commit what has become wanton violence.

The series ends much as it begins for Roman: filming, watching the stories of others through his camera, seeing how D's story ends and saying his goodbyes to Weak and Talia; and, finally, left alone back where he started in Night City. As a protagonist, Roman is far less powerful than David or even the other characters in Edgerunners 2, and his humanity--or, specifically, his organic body--makes up a core component of much of the theme running through the show. Roman's lack of implants, chrome, augmentations and otherwise leaves him mostly on the sidelines of all of the action. He can't see Capri, nor is he affected by her, he can't stop any of the violence or fighting, and he also can't do anything physically to save Talia or others; all he can do is be there for them and show that he cares.

Edgerunners 2 has a consistent theme of storytelling, connections, and communication, and Roman serves as the series heart; without him, the story doesn't work, and his fascination with the camera and movies serves as a vector to cover those ideas and explore them as a work of art. In the final episode, Then Everyone Went Home, Roman again resumes using his camera, but more importantly, actually observes the lives and conflicts of those around him; when he arrives before much of the climax, Capri even teases him, "What, no camera today"? Roman is as much the protagonist as he is the camera, and for the viewer, the point of view for a majority of the story's heart, and also what makes Edgerunners 2 so much different from its predecessor: this is a Night City in which humanity, hope, and connection actually matter.

A Day Late and a Dollar Short

Perhaps the biggest bait and switch that Edgerunners 2 pulls is that of King, whose full name is revealed tobe Weak Kingsley. There's certainly some funny consideration for who in the world names their kid "Weak" even in a cyber dystopian future, but Weak first appears as a shockingly huge, bulging man who seems to be the muscle of the show. Unfortunately for him (and possibly for viewers expecting something different), Weak is suffering from Cyberpsychosis, which leads the job he's on in the first episode to go completely sideways, setting the plot in motion.

It also leads Weak to getting all of his implants removed and downgraded, told he can never chrome out again, and also nearly destitute. In some ways, it seems like Weak's fate is a very tongue in cheek start to the story in the way that David's life, one ruined by debt and ending with his own Cyberpsychosis, is something that could have been avoided with enough money, apparently. Still, Weak finds himself completely at the mercy of Avida, a woman that at first seems to be someone who has passed on, as only Weak sees her in his episodes, but it turns out she is not only very much alive, but needs Weak to find and collect her daughter, Talia.

She ain't who you think she is, literally.

Weak sucks, and he knows it. He spends the series learning not to suck, but it costs him just about everything: his augmentations, his crew, his prestige, his money, and Avida, the woman that continues to selfishly press him to save Talia. She even lies to him, telling him that Talia is his--their--daughter, all to manipulate him into "saving" her (more on that later). In the end, though, Weak really is, well, not weak. He continues perservering, using the second chance he's been given despite all of its flaws, to help Talia, a girl he believes is his daughter, only to become the actual meme itself: he isn't the step dad, he's the dad who stepped up. Rather than being a badass unstoppable berserker, Weak is a schlubby manfailure who ends the series giving up all of the things that held him back to be the person who can do right by someone; in the final climax, he gives up on his obsession with Avida (by literally having her ashes scattered) and his legacy, leaving the jacket of "King" behind. His final line, "let's live!", through tears and sniffling, is hard not to smile at.

I love this dude.

Weak reminds me of a few characters, and when I mentioned that Edgerunners 2 has a Cowboy Bebop vibe to it, it is pretty easy to draw the line between Jet Black and Weak Kingsley, although I suppose one would probably argue that Jet is maybe a bit less of a failman than Weak is, they fulfill a somewhat similar role in the ensemble; I have to admit he also reminds me of Trigun's protagonist Vash, at least from the earlier episodes in which he's a goofier, less surefire hero. As far as an "Ossan" (Older man) character goes, Weak is a fun character whose triumph in the end, that of letting go of his past and vowing to live his own life away from Night City with Talia, feels like the best possible ending for him, as well as strengthening the overall narrative of season 2's focus on humanity.

Payback

Where David Martinez's story is sold as one of righteous fury and an attempt to make a name for one's self against an uncaring city, the story first introduces D's search for revenge as something personal, primal, but ultimately noble: to find out who was responsible for the eradication of the Snake clan from the Badlands that he hails from. What becomes clear is that D is haunted, constantly seeing nightmares of the people that died and the carnage that was left behind int he wake of the assault on his clan. D's eventual meeting with Roman, and their work on creating videos that show D's increasing vigilante action against Arasaka, also brings him into contact with the constructed personality Capri, a digital being that gives David superhuman (bordering on supernatural) powers that he begins to use without a care in the world for what it results in.

D's quest for revenge at any costs soon leads him and Roman to split, primarily over the interference of a woman named Yupi, whose own personal quest for vengeance against Arasaka pushes D further and further into the path of violence. While revenge narratives are rarely ever "pro" revenge, D's story is even more blatant about it as his mood and demeanor changes. Yupi's influence really just seems to accelerate what was already happening, or perhaps bound to happen, as D doesn't really seem to have much of a plan besides taking "revenge" for his clan. When confronted by Roman about it, he simply says that his killing spree is because only "he" can see "them", the ghosts of his clan that haunt him.

The grand irony, sadly, is that D's clan dies because of him: as revealed late into the narrative, D was a person of interest to Arasaka for a project related to implanting constructed identities. This reveal makes D spiral, furthering the fact that his revenge has long since moved past righteous and well into simply, well, murder at a grand scale. But while that's certainly the basic narrative form of most revenge stories, that "revenge is bad", Edgerunners does add a few wrinkles to this element through another Snake clan member: Omi.

Roman did this woman dirty filming this.

Omi shows up in the back half of the show, after viewers are led to believe that the Snake clan has been wiped out to a single entity, D, which instead leaves us with questions of how many people actually died and how many survived. Omi, unlike D, has opted to try and make her life about more than just seeking revenge, and their initial tense meeting leads to further conflict down the line. But rarely in a revenge story is the person seeking revenge directly confronted by an equally wronged party, asking them what the point of what they are doing serves. D, unfortunately, refuses to see the forest for the trees, or at least, has deluded himself into believing that his revenge is all that matters.

But when Roman captures his smile following his first day with Capri, the actual truth is something that D refuses to acknowledge until the end of the series, and until it is perhaps too late for him to have pursued a different path: that he could have been happy, that he could have lived a life of his own, had he refused to believe that revenge was all that his life, that his surviving, was good for. In the end, D's fate is implied heavily to have burned bright and out, but perhaps his ending is also that he reached the stars with Capri, becoming a legend who blazed his own trail.

I Saw the TV Glow

The final member of the protagonists is Talia, the 15 year old girl who is seemingly obsessed with having her body augmented and upgraded with chrome; when we first meet Talia, she's shown to have replaced her arms, legs, and mouth with various types of implants and augments, giving her an almost insect-like quality to the way she approaches Roman. The animations of Talia eating are... pretty wild, and probably best experienced rather than explained, but Talia's narrative is one of self-determination in the face of a world that seems dead set on telling one how to live.

That's right, Talia's a big ol' trans allegory character. And, as I mentioned in my other review, this isn't something that Cyberpunk 2077 has always handled particularly well. There are some bumps in the road with Talia as well, but not in a way that doesn't actually accomplish the allegory in a compelling way. If anything, the messy and slightly indirect nature of the allegory makes it work, and as the relationship between Talia, Avida, and Kiril (her father, and also a dickhead) is laid bare, it becomes easier to sympathize with why Talia has wanted to live her life as who she wants to be, rather than who others want her to be.

Kiril is the obvious villain, the controlling and uncaring corpo father who simply wants Talia for his own ends; her apparent ability to merge with Capri is more about his corporate success and gain than it is saving Talia from the unnamed disease that is eating away at her organic body. Kiril is, if anything, the less interesting of the two parents when it comes to the trans allegory, because he is simply an uncaring father who doesn't see his child for who they are: she is not a person to Kiril, and her desires, dreams, or thoughts don't matter to him. She is a means to an end, she is property, and her body is his to control and mold into what he wants.

The shocker, really, is Avida. The story starts with Avida worried about Talia and wanting her brought home safely, leading her to offer to pay Weak and lie to him that she is his daughter. Avida's concern seems genuine, and her sorrow over Talia's illness seems like it will lead to a narrative reconciliation where Talia's pursuit of augmentation is not that she wishes to shun her mother, but that the two are simply trying to pursue what they feel is best for Talia's life. The reality is... complicated. In the final act, Avida is asked to select a new body for Talia, one that she can, supposedly, be "transferred" into. Avida hesitates, complaining that she will no longer be "her" Talia, that the body she has is not "hers", and by "hers", she means HERS. Avida, much like her odious husband, similarly views Talia as something that belongs to her, and something that should look and resemble what she wants, namely, the "Baby" she gave birth to and the image of "Talia" she constructed.

Perhaps it may seem obvious, but this doubled up set of rejection for Talia's identity and personhood is pretty common for many trans people; parents who can only see 'their little boy' or 'little girl', who worry that 'you're going to make a change you can't take back' not out of concern for the individual, but for what they feel they are losing in the process. the trans person's self-determination,  happiness, and quality of life aren't considered in the equation, because their identity doesn't fully belong to them: it belongs to their "family", the same one that wants to control, reject, or restrict them.

But then there is Roman, and by extension, Weak.

Weak rises up to be the "dad" Talia never had, a person who knows her experiences and the fears and concerns, while also trying to offer her camaraderie and support. There's a fun throughline to viewing Weak as a similar trans allegory, trying to build a bridge between trans elder and trans junior between the two and their rocky relationship as it unfolds over the course of the show. At the end, as he tearfully drives them into the sunset, it is hard to view them as anything but father and daughter, even with her fate left up in the air; whatever it is, she gets to live it on her own terms.

Roman, her "boyfriend", is similarly interesting. Whereas other people see Talia for what she "is" to them, Roman simply sees her as what he initially captured on his camera: striking, beautiful, and perfect. Roman and Talia's interactions are sweet and fluffy while also tragic, the sort of young love that's doomed by the narrative in numerous ways. Talia even confesses to liking Roman, while he remains unable to answer well until the final moments of the show, and their "date" at a drive-in is almost shockingly wholesome for a series like Cyberpunk. Before she drives off with Weak, Roman confesses that she was always perfect, which she quips back at with "what a line". To Roman, Talia is who she is, with no expectations or demands: she is just perfect.

I, Robot

Capri is the character that haunts the background of Edgerunners 2, a constructed identity who doesn't make her way into the show until the middle third of the story. We get bits and pieces of how Capri, or Capricorn, was made, and what she can do, but she serves almost as a magical MacGuffin more than she does exist as an individual character. She has motives and wants, albeit again not fully explored or identified; what we do know is that she seems to really want to reach "the sky".

Capri's actual point of interest to me, though, is just how Studio Trigger she is. Capri resembles a character out of Panty and Stocking with Garterbelt, a sort of stocky, cartoonishly shaped amalgam of colors and shapes that resembles a feminine form. She's capricious and playful, but similarly juvenile as many depictions of artificial life tends to be. Her biggest benefit to the show is that she allows Cyberpunk 2077, even with all of its sci-fi ridiculousness, to escape the bounds of reality; when she's tagging along with D, his hair spikes up and gives him the ability to do just about anything, and when Talia merges with her later, she begins morphing into a Tetsuo the Iron Man horror, at one point resembling a cobbled together cockroach. She provides the "anime" to the animated series in a few fashions, even if her overall narrative themes aren't explored much beyond establishing what she is.

The Island of Dr. Moreau

Before moving on to the final part of this overarching review/analysis, I have to spend some time talking about my favorite character. This character doesn't show up for more than 2/3rds of the series, and has less screentime than just about any character other than Capri, but I absolutely love this vile little cockroach of a woman. Since you're probably only reading this if you already watched the show, I bet you can immediately guess who I'm thinking about, but if you're unsure, I'm talking about the one, the only, Kyoko.

Look at this fucking creature.

Kyoko is the character responsible for a good portion of the plot of Edgerunners 2 happening, and she's doing so dressed in god's ugliest fit (seriously, those chunky pink croc-like sandals are something else); she is the primary person behind Capri's creation, she is also the person who steals Capri back from King's crew, and she has knowledge of what happened to D's clan (and similarly, who Talia is). She is a vile, awful person, a "mad scientist" type who sees no obstacle in her pursuit of her creation's success, which also makes her a fascinating and entertaining little problem. In theory, Kyoko is an antagonist who only wishes to get Capri back and have her fully under her control, but she also wants Capri to exist and succeed, which ironically brings her to saving the day with the rest of the crew at the end of the series.

Look at that hair.

I love morally terrible characters like Kyoko,  because when they're done well, they add layers and depth to the cast. Kyoko would very likely never be friends with anyone in the cast, and D even tries to kill her at one point for her role in what happened to his clan; she also causes Talia to be kidnapped by her father at the end, and yet it is, at least to me, impossible to hate her.  She dies, like all terrible people in media tend to, or at least we are led to believe she does; no matter what, D and Capri bring her along for their 'final show' to give her a send off in style for what she made possible, and I find it hard to believe Kyoko would want it any other way.

Robot Carnival

Although I've spent a good portion of this (okay, almost all of it) talking about the cast, themes, and plot, I want to give Kai Ikarashi his flowers: Edgerunners 2 is a beautiful show. It is not the most technically impressive animated series I've ever seen, in that it is looking to blow the roof off of the place with set pieces, but instead it wants to utilize animation and film techniques in ways that animation allows that aren't always possible with live action. And that is also to say that the animation here IS very good, some of Studio Trigger's best, all framed around coherent and visually interesting storytelling. There is a lot of care here to make Night City feel alive; characters drink and eat, they travel, they live lives, and the show does its best to give us small pockets of that life between the bigger set pieces.

Some of the most interesting pieces are those of D's nightmares and fears, which are often rendered as completely flat, dual or monotone colored sequences, often using bright primary colors and white. Capri is similarly colorful and garish, making every scene she appears in almost feel like it was from the wrong series, given how she clashes with the overall aesthetic. Ikarashi's vision is very clear, and appreciating the show visually for it adds a lot of depth to the entire production; since the series has so much it wants to invest into thinking about film, art, and creation, it becomes clear that the production had to similarly consider ways to show that off.

In the climax of the show, one of the most stark scenes is that of D picking up a camera, aiming it at Roman. it is the first, and only, time the that we see Roman on film in the way he's captured others, revealing just how small, vulnerable, and human he is. And that, when he needs to express earnestly to Roman in their final conversation, Ikarashi cuts to a final shot of D looking over the top of the camera at Roman, making direct eye contact with him, calling back to Roman's words in the first episode: that the screen, the camera, creates a barrier between the viewer and the creator.

Seeya, sunshine.

Cinema Paradiso

I've spoken a lot about the cast, primarily as vectors to explore the ways in which their stories provide interesting, unique insights into what Edgerunners 2 wants to do. A lot of this is due to the initial reactions I've noticed about the series, which is that people seem to have wanted Edgerunners 1 again, or a story that is similarly bleak or dark; Edgerunners 2 is plenty dark, but it has a very different message and scope that it wants to explore. Edgerunners 2 is a story about stories, about connections, and about humanity, set in a world in which people care very little for each other and life is cheap.

It feels difficult to separate Edgerunners 2 from the world in which it was produced; early on in the show, Roman discusses how Braindances, the Cyberpunk 2077 "entertainment" form that is beamed into one's brain, lacks the same type of craft and connection that film and movies can produce. Roman wants to make movies, because the artifice of making movies is what gives them their humanity: a person has to film it, a person has to watch it. And it was impossible to read this scene as neutral in a period in which AI videos are clogging up social media, sites likes YouTube, and other social media apps, soulless, talentless, craftless things that are not made by people and, truthfully, are not made to even be enjoyed by people, but instead numbers: views, clicks, likes, whatever.

Yupi, the woman that inserts herself between Roman and D, fills a similar role: the pursuit of a creative medium not for what it says or conveys,  but for how it can divide and create capital. Yupi says she cares about taking down Arasaka, but the reality is that her selfish desire is purely nihilistic and self-serving: she loves seeing D get violent, she loves the money it brings her, the fame, the crowd, the success, all of which she begins to trade for a loss of humanity; people are killed, people that don't even have anything to do with Arasaka, and all of them are turned into spectacle, bereft of meaning. Of course, media lead times can't predict events, but a show that grapples with the destructive carnivale of protest turning into little more than pornographic displays of violence, of sound and fury meaning nothing, certainly couldn't land at a better time than it did; and, realistically, unlike many other narratives that grapple with protest and violence, Edgerunners 2 doesn't even try to tow the line that violence, protest, revolt and fighting are not the answer, just that, for the Yupi's of the world, it has little to do with what is being fought for, and all to do with creating an entertaining mess.

If there is anything that Edgerunners 2 wants to say, it is as noted before: that humans live through telling, sharing, and remembering stories. It is how we convince ourselves to do things, whether we're lying to ourselves or not, and it is how we connect with others. The stories we tell ourselves are just as important as those we tell others, and they are also the way in which we become known to other people. What it means to be alive, to live, is to create and share what we create, even if those things are words we share with other people. If anything, Edgerunners also has something to say about fidelity and honesty, that what we see on the screen can tell the truth, depending on how the camera is controlled. Roman's films carry an air of nostalgic passion for the past of making movies, but in the show itself, his films capture the honest, quiet moments of people's lives: D's smile, Talia's joy, his father's craft. As the story draws to a close, Talia, Weak, and Roman all come to their own conclusions on what to do with their lives, to prove that their lives were indeed worth living and pursuing, and that life is a process of stories to be told, shared, and retold; as Roman runs off screen to continue pursuing his dreams, the camera pans up, showing a Night City sky filled not with dark, dystopian shadows, but bright, individual stars.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2
content:
This review contains no spoilers, and talks broadly about the plot and themes of the show without providing specifics. If you want more in-depth information, well, stay tuned choom. 

Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2 opens with a broad gambit: what if a sequel can actually be better than the original? There's some precedent for it, certainly, but sequels tend to struggle with the legacy of what came before them, and in Edgerunners 2's case, that is a pretty impressive wall to climb. But if I told you that Edgerunners 2 only wanted to be better than the first series, I think it would be doing both of them a disservice. Perhaps to get the controversial out of the way in the intro: if you are a fan of cyberpunk themes, Cyberpunk the game, and also the original series, then Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2 is an easy sell. But exactly why takes a bit more discussion and delving into what the sequel is wanting to do and what makes it successful, and perhaps if you've been on the fence or are curious, this review can give some push to giving the new series a try.

Last Chance for a Slow Dance

Edgerunners 2's primary protagonist is a young boy named Roman, whose obsession with film serves as both a framing and thematic device for the entire series. Roman is obsessed with the concept of film being a superior form of media than Braindances, a lost art form that can connect the viewer and the creator through the forced disconnect of the camera. The show regularly utilizes a filter to create a retro film grain effect, as well as sound mixing to make things sound like one might expect when recorded on a handheld camera. Roman wants to be a director, a creator, someone who proves the value of film in a world that sees it as nostalgic entertainment at best.

That runs paralell to a bigger theme in the second season, that of humanity in a world filled with artifice and implants. Of the 4 protagonists at the center of Edgerunners, Roman is the only one who has minimal implants and chrome: King is an older Edgerunner who faces down the reality of life after cyberpsychosis, Talia is an burgeoning implant addict, and the mysterious D seems more than happy to use hacking implants and more to get to the bottom of his revenge plot. All of these characters end up circling each other through fate, happenstance, and of course, The Narrative, but the one who remains slightly at a distance and slowly sucked into the center of it is Roman.

Early in the series, Roman's love of film but need to live gets him tangled up in the web of the others, and the series continually makes an interesting contrast between Roman the person and Roman the director; forced to actually take part in what he's recording, Roman's point of view to the audience shifts from watching his actions and watching his camera. Much like the artificial world of hacking and implants, Roman finds himself also having to separate himself from viewing and acting.

10:15 On a Saturday Night

Edgerunners 2's major theme, as perhaps rote as it might sound, is humanity and the ties that bind. The opening song, 10:15 Saturday Night by the Cure, is accompanied by a flat color montage of the characters and world that we're going to view, black, white, and big flashy blocky colors fly at us. Director Kai Ikarashi absolutely understood the assignment, because one of the first impulses I had while watching the show is that it reminded me of Cowboy Bebop: grainy, colorful, and combining flat and dynamic aesthetics in a way that is both "Cyberpunk" while doing something original.

Like Bebop, and perhaps unlike Edgerunners, Edgerunners 2 is an ensemble cast story that doesn't immediately rush to push the characters together; by the midpoint of the series the characters have all started to enter closer and closer orbit with one another, inevitably drawn together because they have to be, and it is perhaps one of the things that I think will instantly turn off people who are looking specifically for Edgerunners "Again". Ikarashi and writer Bartosz Sztybor have done an interesting job of ensuring that this series is not just a referendum on the first, nor is it doing the same things again, while also dropping small hints, narrative concepts, and webs of connection that do tie the two of them together; after all, this all does take place in the same setting and city.

The show plays with the concept of film, storytelling, and connections as a driving narrative factor, while also heavily playing with musical layers. Every episode is a song title, tied to the themes of the show and the episodes events, and across the 10 episodes of season 2 there's a deep investment in those connections tying back to the concept of what makes us human, or just what it means to live, be remembered, and remembering. Roman is obsessed with filming the world around him, Talia wants to be the version of herself she feels only she understands, King lingers in his obsessions with the past and its consequences, and D wants revenge in the memory of others. Without trying to compare the two, I found Edgerunners 2's cast far more dynamic than the first series; while David, Rebecca and Lucy are all fun and amazing characters, their story is an entirely different examination of the Cyberpunk setting, and in 2, we have one that even the game itself struggles with: living.

Then Everyone Went Home

Living isn't something the Cyberpunk universe has always done a fantastic job of exploring, and in a lot of broader senses, something that cyberpunk media doesn't always engage with either. We certainly get numerous novels, movies, games, comics, and more that conceptualize the dystopian worlds of cyberpunk universes, often filled with wet dreams of tech run amok and evil corporations, but they don't often build a lot of grounding in what living is actually like; if one were to go by Edgerunners or Cyberpunk 2077, the answer apparently is that one lives in total misery until your life is summarily ended with a bang or a splat.

Edgerunners 2 takes the somewhat initial lower stakes and point of view to show that, well, people have to actually live in this universe, and that life is not as pointless, brutish, and short as it may seem otherwise. Roman lives with his father, goes shopping for groceries, and tries to make a living with his films; King, despite his Edgerunning, has connections to people and relationships, while D is someone whose loss of these things makes him driven to exact revenge.

Talia is perhaps the most interesting character, a woman obsessed with her pursuit of transhuman perfection; it is pretty difficult to not read Talia's struggles with identity and her pursuits as a trans allegory, with the reminder that the Cyberpunk universe has had some... spotty history with that concept. In Edgerunners 2, at least, Talia's struggle is put forward as one of a person who wishes to be free to be the person they believe they want to be, and at times the allegory works and at others it doesn't; remember, Cyberpunk is a world in which Cyberpsychosis is real, which does mute some of her zeal for changing her body with the idea that it will literally kill her, eventually. Still, she's an interesting and frustrating character, the type that you want to both yell at and support with how she acts, in the way that good but flawed characters often do.

There are more characters, revealed in the midpoint, that shift the story into new directions, but I'll avoid revealing them except to say that one of them is an abominable little creature that also is very entertaining, and another that allows you to really feel the Studio Trigger energy from their character design, if you're familiar with their wider body of work. By the end, I was vastly in love with this cast, and while the finality of the first series made it feel like a done and settled affair, I wouldn't mind seeing more of these characters again, but I can also deeply respect the story that is told.

Give Me Another Day

The animation of Edgerunners 2 is some of Trigger's best, bar none; if anything, watching the show for the animation and cinematography alone is a treat. I've had a pretty mixed reception to many of Trigger's works, and the legacy that preceded them in places like Studio Gainax, but one thing I've always held respect for is that Trigger knows they are working in the realm of cartoons. While Edgerunners 2 tells a grounded story in the Cyberpunk universe, it isn't afraid to get cartoonish, particularly with the above mentioned character.

Even aside from them, there's fun uses of wipes, smears, and forced perspective animation that shows off some of the reasons why animation can do things that live action camerawork just is not capable of. At the end of episode one, there's a sequence of fluid monochromatic animation that feels electric to watch, and later episodes produce eye-pleasing action sequences; one that I particularly enjoyed is an almost comical segment in which disembodied hands hold all manner of guns out of a car window while an endless stream of palm-trees scrolls by in the background on a flat color backdrop; the combination of cartoonish comedy of it with the action happening just works together to create an engaging sequence, which the series continues to replicate.

Ikarashi is primarily known as a key animator, having only directed two works so far in his career, with Edgerunners 2 being the second (the first, Heavenly Delusion, actually has a lot in common with the type of style and stories he likes to tell). But this is a man whose animation credits are on the likes of SSSS. Gridman, Promare, and Mob Psycho 100, which is to say that his pedigree for style and animation tricks certainly lives up to that pedigree. D's flashbacks and nightmares are presented in striking primary flat colors, the film grain on Roman's camera feels deeply creative and well researched, and the majority of the series has that realistic, grounded feeling that the best animation creates: that even though these are not real actors in real places, they still feel and act human.

Edgerunners 2 is a triumph in a lot of ways: it has amazing animation, a great story, good characters, and a banging soundtrack to accompany it, but it also manages to live up to the expectation of a sequel to Edgerunners. And frankly, if you just want more of David, Rebecca, and Lucy, may I suggest you watch the cutscenes of the Wuthering Waves collaboration instead? Because they were also written by the main author and serve as a fascinating epilogue from Lucy's point of view, and perhaps if that is all you wanted, will suffice. But if you're looking for a great exploration of what it means to live and exist in the world of Cyberpunk, of what it means to be a human, of connection, film, and stories, then Edgerunners 2 is where it's at, choomfie.

title: Games Industry News Roundup- October 20th, 2026
content:
Here at Tabletop Battles, we know that it’s hard to keep track of all the news happening all the time in the games industry. So much is always going on, all over the place, all the time. With games of all sorts, and their related media, being an informed gamer can feel impossible some days. 

That's why every week, we help you stay in the know by rounding up five of the biggest recent stories in the gaming and gaming-related pop culture sphere in the Games Industry News Roundup. Our trusty news boy, Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson, is right here at the very real, and cool TTB newsdesk with the scoop.

Total War Game Pulled from Digital Platforms Due to Quality Issues

The Total War games by Creative Assembly are no strangers to buggy launches, which makes sense on some level considering the sheer scale of the games. There is a fine line between a game being described simply as buggy, however, and a game being in a broken state, and the latest Total War release looks to have landed on the wrong side of that line. In response, the Creative Assembly Team announced last week that it would be pulling Total War: Shogun 2 - Complete Edition from digital storefronts for an indeterminate period of time, while the team addresses and fixes the title.

“We’re aware that Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards,” Creative Assembly wrote in an announcement alongside the game’s publisher, Sega. “We’ve seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be.”

“As a result we are working with platform holders to remove the game from sale and to reinstate the original game while we investigate the issues. Existing owners will still be able to access and play the game.”

Alongside a myriad of performance issues, the game was widely criticized by its playerbase for the use of generative AI upscaling of assets from the original game, such as unit cards and cutscenes, which caused noticeable issues that are trademark problems of AI art such as extra fingers, inconsistent details, and armor melting into the skin of samurai unit cards.

The Shogun 2 remaster released on October 13th, 2026, replacing the original version of the game on Steam with a new and much more expensive price tag of $40. The old version of the game has been reinstated while Creative Assembly works with Mataboo, a Polish studio which helped with the remastered game’s development, to resolve the issues the title faced on launch, though neither Creative Assembly or Sega have directly stated that this includes the AI assets.

The joint duo of CA and Sega conclude their statement by writing, “We are working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements, and ensure Shogun 2 – Complete Edition meets the quality standards players expect from Total War.”

At time of writing, there is no news about when Shogun 2 - Complete Edition will return to digital storefronts.

Bernhardt: Worth noting for transparency that we did run a review of this game for the site, and our reviewer did not experience the performance issues that many other outlets did; that said, the news story around this game has well overtaken any individual review of the title.

Credit: Epic Games

Epic Taunts Steam with New Upgrade, Gets Owned Immediately

It’s a sad truth of the world that those who deserve to step on rakes simply don’t step on them, somehow avoiding public embarrassment for their hubris and learning no lessons in the process. This makes it all the more joyous in those rare instances where we do see rakes get stepped on in a spectacular manner, as Epic Games did this past week. Epic is leaning hard into its AI development, boasting last week that thanks to its “vibe coding” and AI tools the studio was able to make the Epic Games Store launcher faster than Steam, only to find that Steam had already boosted its own performance to be faster than Epic.

In the original post, Epic boasted “Programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look.” Epic Games confirmed to IGN in an interview that “vibe coding” was a cute way to say “programmed with AI”, as the company said that it used AI programming to allow for the Epic Games store to massively boost it’s startup performance to the point where it was now 46% faster on launch than it’s main competitor, Steam. Epic’s data showed that Steam’s startup time on PC launch was about 10.07 seconds, while the Epic store now launched in 5.47 seconds.

This push for AI comes from the very top of Epic, who have leaned so hard into the tech that it’s delaying the release of a Marvel and Disney shooter in order to focus on AI-first coding. Tim Sweeny, Epic’s CEO, posted on social media earlier this month that “ We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration.”

Users quickly found that Epic’s bragging was premature, as Steam developer Valve had rolled out an upgrade earlier that same day which included better performance and a much faster launch time for Steam. According to user testing, the updated Steam client now launched from startup in 5.23 seconds, which is ever so slightly faster than the ‘vibe coded’ Epic Games Store.

While Valve has not made any statement on its own internal development process for Steam, nor any statement regarding Epic’s attempt to dunk on them, the update is a major embarrassment for Epic, who seem to have burned many fans with its plans to focus on AI first coding while still coming up short to compared to Steam.

Credit: Osprey Games

Osprey Games Lets Go of Board and Card Game Range After Sale Falls Through

In the world of Tabletop Games, things are a bit more grim. Osprey Publishing has reportedly let go of it’s entire board and card game development teams, Osprey Games, and cancelled its booth at the upcoming Spiel Essen convention in Germany, as it’s been unable to find a buyer following selloff from its original publisher Bloomsbury Publishing.

Bloomsbury originally sold off the board and card game division of Osprey in May of this year, citing a “strategic refocus on book publishing”. Since then Osprey Publishing, which primarily focuses on publishing historical wargaming rulebooks, has been looking for a buyer for Osprey Games and its titles, which include the popular Undaunted series of board games.

After months of searching, however, it seems as though Osprey has been unsuccessful in finding anyone to purchase the games division, and sources from within the company told BoardGameWire that “all our colleagues who exclusively worked on creating and manufacturing our board and card games have now left the company”.

According to the report, Osprey Publishing is no longer looking for a buyer for the entire department, but has shifted to to instead seek out a buyer just for its board and card game lines. This could be complicated by ownership rights over Osprey Games catalogue, as the designer contracts from Osprey Games restrict the sale of the games rights to a third party.

Osprey Publishing has not made any direct comment regarding this, stating only that “The contractual arrangements relating to Osprey Games are confidential, so we’re not able to share details of specific terms or comment on potential outcomes. We appreciate that these questions are important to designers and other partners, and we’ll share further information with those directly involved as soon as we’re able to.”

Credit: United Wizards of the Coast

Wizards Leadership Fails to Voluntarily Recognize the D&D and Magic Union

Last week, the Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering teams at Wizards of the Coast made huge waves with the announcement that they intended to follow in the footsteps of the Arena development team and unionize under the United Wizards of the Coast union (UWOTC), demanding better wages and worker protections. At the time, UWOTC asked for the leadership at Wizards and parent company Hasbro to voluntarily recognize their union by October 13th, rather than have to go to a union election. Wizards and Hasbro have since declined to recognize the union, and has since put out a statement saying regarding its decision, forcing the union election process.

“Yesterday, Wizards informed us that it doesn’t intend to voluntarily recognize the D&D or Studio X units of our union ahead of a vote,” UWOTC wrote on social media on October 14th. “We remain committed to creating a workplace focused on wellness, transparency, and collaboration by winning our coming election.”

Wizards would also release a statement regarding their decision, writing in an internal email obtained by Wargamer that “we are best able to keep building great games and a great place to work by working directly with employees, not through unions. In this regard, Wizards is not neutral on the question of unionization.”

While Wizards and Hasbro state later in the email that they intend to honor the results of any election from their teams, both companies were accused of engaging in union busting tactics earlier this year during the original formation of the UWOTC by the Magic the Gathering: Arena team.

With voluntary recognition efforts having failed, the teams at Wizards will now engage in a union vote by employees to ratify the union, which will likely take place in November.

Credit: Games Workshop/Karl Kopinski

Trench Crusade Developers Launch Crowdfunding Campaign for Warhammer Artist

Last year, legendary Warhammer artist Karl Kopinsky suffered a major stroke following routine treatment for his myeloma, which left him unable to draw for some time. Following this news, the community rallied behind Kopinsky to assist with his medical bills, and it looks like the team at Trench Crusade is leading the charge again to financially assist the popular artist by announcing the launch of a new STL campaign on MyMiniFactory to benefit Kopinski.

The campaign, which is set to launch on MyMiniFactory later this year, was organized by Factory Fortress and MyMiniFactory as a collaboration between multiple wargaming studios and artists in support of Kopinski. Those who back the campaign will receive a new and exclusive model for Trench Crusade, which has not yet been revealed, as well as a large collection of additional STLs created by the collaborating artists.

Tuomas Pirinen, lead designer at Factory Fortress for Trench Crusade, wrote on the Trench Crusade Facebook page “Karl is my friend as well as my housemate during my GW days, so I am so glad we can help him and his family. Get your hands on a brand new Trench Crusade miniature and help out an artist who has done so much for us over the years!”

Kopinski worked at Games Workshop from 1998-2005 as an artist and is responsible for a number of extremely popular pieces of art, such as the iconic art for Codex: Eye of Terror. Since then, Kopinski has been working as a prolific freelance artist in the gaming sphere. Kopinski’s stroke in 2025 left him paralyzed on his left side, and though he was able to regain movement he had to teach himself how to draw again. While his recovery is going well, it is still ongoing, and proceeds from the MyMiniFactory campaign will go directly towards these medical bills.

title: MTG Star Trek reveals unstoppable Borg Cube card and exponentially spreading Tribbles
content:
Wizards of the Coast has just unleashed a tidal wave of spoilers for the upcoming MTG Star Trek set. Among them were a bunch of spaceships and a Jean Luc Picard that can fetch and charge them up, a lot of doubling effects, and some intriguing sagas named after specific episodes. There's a lot to talk about here, but we're just going to look at four cards here with truly interesting effects.

First up we have The Borg Cube, an expensive spaceship which luckily has affinity for artifacts, which will make it much more castable in a Borg deck. On the turn that you play it, this is just an overcosted removal spell, but if you're able to get it up to 12 charge counters it becomes very scary indeed.

For starters, it's a flying 6/6 that gives all your other artifact creatures flying, letting you swoop in the skies with impunity. On top of that it lets you assimilate the creature you exiled, bringing it back onto the board on your side as a Borg artifact. Plus, if The Borg Cube isn't dealt with it will kill again - each turn where you don't assimilate when you attack, you get to exile your next victim. Overall, a fantastic card, I'm only sad it can't go in the command zone.

Secondly, we have Q, Stacking the Deck. In terms of reading experience, this one's as confusing as any meeting with Q, but here's more or less what it does. You exile a card from your library, and from that point on, any card in your hand can be used as though it's a copy of that card. I bet there's some tricksy ways to abuse this!

Thirdly, it's Troubling Tribbles, a multiplying alien menace which creates more copies of itself each turn - as do those copies. Now it's not just the green players you have to worry about making an unending, exponentially growing horde. The only comfort is that the Tribbles are 0/1s, so their controller will need to put a little work in to find a way to make use of them.

Finally, we have The Kobayashi Maru Scenario, the famous 'no-win' training simulation. Basically, this is blue Demonic Pact. You get to pick a powerful effect each turn, but if it's still on the board in four turns, you'll lose the game. Rather than boons bargained for with demons, the flavor words give the impression of an officer trying all available options, then giving up and having to abandon ship.

Check out the Debut video for yourself to see all the spoilers just shown off - though I'd say you've viewed the cream of the crop already.

title: Warhammer 40k 11th edition has a Deathwatch problem
content:
The Paris Wargame Expo kicked off on October 17, and so began our first major Warhammer 40k tournament weekend since the Space Marines codex dropped on the 3rd. The biggest development is that this new marine-powered meta seems to have an issue with the Deathwatch, specifically with them showing up in Space Marine armies and being just a little busted.

Some Deathwatch players were understandably a bit grumpy that the 1DP detachment with their name on it was actually a detachment for other Space Marine players that let them use all the Deathwatch's best toys. Now the evidence suggests that the Deathwatch Support detachment, giving other chapters 500 points of DW to play with, is really damn strong.

Throw some Deathwatch Terminators with their extra plasma cannons into, say, an Ultramarine army, and it turns out it does wonders for their win rate. The Deathwatch Support rules let you throw Precision, Sustained Hits or Lethal Hits onto the units, giving them an absurd amount of killiness, even before you load on your other Space Marine buffs and detachments.

While Space Marines as a whole seemed to be in a pretty perfect spot, with a 51% win rate last weekend, Goo- I mean, Tabletop Battles, ran the numbers and concluded that Marines with Deathwatch in tow were winning 69% of their games. Yowza. Deathwatch alone did decently too - but appeared in such low numbers that we can't really draw conclusions from the available data.

It seems likely that if this pattern continues, Games Workshop will step in and make some tweaks. It shouldn't be too hard to figure out a fix. You could add heavy weapon limitations to the detachment, make it more expensive, stop other detachment rules from working with the Deathwatch units - there's all sorts of options. In other words, don't drop everything and buy a bunch of models with the plan to dominate competitive tables with this technique.

Another high-performing Warhammer 40k faction in the past couple of weeks is the World Eaters, using lots of Berzerkers, while the Astra Militarum is doing dismally - win rates below 40%. Auspex Tactics just released a breakdown if you want all the latest data.

title: Why I hope Travis Willingham never comes back to Critical Role campaign four
content:
It has been four months since the death of Teor Pridesire. As well as being one of Critical Role campaign 4's biggest story beats to date, it also structurally changed the Dungeons and Dragons game. Three tables became two. And, personally, I think the campaign is a lot more watchable for it.

For a while now, Critical Role campaign four has had a problem of breadth. Expecting 13 actors, however talented, to share a spotlight means some characters fall to the wayside. There's fewer chances to build relationships with a split party, and that lessens investment in their development. Basically, the more characters there are to keep up with, the less time I have to learn to love them.

I mentioned this problem in a recent op ed about the campaign's budding romances. Tyranny and Wick's emotional relationship is engrossing, because they spent a lot of time at the same table, building up to a shared story beat. In contrast, Murray and Kattigan's romance, which bloomed while the two spent months at entirely different tables, felt rushed and flat. The storylines actively suffer when players don't have a chance to collaborate.

What's worse, before the Convergence arc, many characters had no relationship at all. Hal and Tyranny were basically strangers until the Soldiers table disbanded. Heck, in last week's episode, Occtis literally pointed out how little reason characters like Bolaire and Kattigan have to care about him.

Kattigan quickly followed this up by instigating a personal moment between him and the Wizard. And there lies the hidden benefit of reducing table count. The Convergence, and the more intimate tables that followed, have been a chance for the party to really get to know each other.

This has indirectly solved a lot of the campaign's other problems. There are no longer any 'background' characters in the party. Quieter team members like Vaelus and Kattigan are thrust to the forefront more often. Both have had more character moments than ever post-Convergence, and it makes me care about them far more.

Plus, there have been zero filler episodes since The Convergence. This has more to do with the careful planning of Brennan Lee Mulligan, but jumping between fewer tables certainly keeps our attention on the action.

For me, Critical Role does its best storytelling when it focuses on character dynamics in great detail. Episode 39 didn't do much to advance the plot, but the relationship development is what made it a delight to watch. Not every episode can be about the power of friendship, but I'd like to see this attention to detail - to characters as individuals - continue.

That's why, when Occtis chose to be a Wizard instead of a Lord, and not to create a new table, I breathed a sigh of relief. It's why I believe 13 players is simply too many cooks. This current arc has 11 players (while Aabria Iyengar takes some leave). It could support 12, with six players at each table, but I don't think it can support 13.

That means somebody must be cut, and I'm afraid it's you, Travis Willingham. Teor Pridesire was the least directly relevant to the overall story. A new character would likely be more involved, but if I have to choose between the current cast and a character that doesn't exist yet, I know which way I'm leaning.

Travis recently admitted he hadn't prepared a back-up character yet, or thought about re-entering the campaign. Personally, I hope his return never comes. It's nothing against him as an actor or a person. I'd just like campaign four to be slightly less ambitious, not more.

Got your own opinions on Critical Role? Share them in the Wargamer Discord. Or, if you want to do your own roleplaying, why not check out our guides to D&D classes and D&D races?

title: For the Gods is a divine board game of Greek myth, but it's one step short of epic
content:
Our Verdict

For the Gods! is smooth sailing, with approachable, airtight area majority rules. Rough seas make the best sailors, though, and the game doesn't forget to offer tense strategic decisions. It's not as complex or memorable as some others of this genre, but it's an excellent gateway with an entertaining bag-building spin. Plus, it's simply divine to behold.

Pros
  • Visually lovely
  • Simple yet brutal strategy
  • Beginner-friendly, but fun for veterans
Cons
  • Less fun at two players
  • Relies a lot on luck
  • Theme feels superficial

For the Gods! is the latest title from a trio of star-studded board game designers. Between them, Trevor Benjamin (Mandala, Resist!, Undaunted), Brett J. Gilbert (Mandala, Divinare), and David Thompson (Undaunted, Resist!) have a small army of awards and nominations. That means, for their next project, expectations are sky-high.

That's fitting for a board game about the Greek Gods, though it doesn't take place on cloudy Mount Olympus. Instead, two to four people play as these deities' human worshippers. Your goals are much more mortal: sail the Aegean archipelago, and build taller temples than your religious rivals.

This is an area majority game whose simple rules are as smooth as Grecian marble, but as rich as a wine-dark sea. The core engine is an efficient bag-building mechanic. Everyone starts the game with 24 stones in their bag (with zero to three pips printed on top), and you'll begin with a starting hand of five, hidden behind a privacy screen.

Each turn, you'll choose whether to visit a new region on the stunningly vibrant board. Each stop on your voyage costs a stone, which you'll return to the bag. Once you've reached your intended port, you can choose to establish, elevate, or dedicate a temple.

Establishing means building a fresh temple in that region, while elevating extends an existing structure. When establishing, simply grab a base, and place any number of tiles with matching pips on top. If the region has a god token lying around, throw it straight in your bag.

These god tokens come into play when you dedicate a temple. You can dedicate as part of an establish or elevate action, and it allows you to place a single god token on top of your temple. This adds a fancy cornice, which looks snazzy, but mainly exists to show the value of the pips beneath. More importantly, though, dedicating your temple triggers that god's power.

Four to six random gods form your pantheon, depending on player count. Dedication lets them shake the earth and seas in different divine ways. Athena swaps the location of two temples on a single island, while Ares steals a god token from a rival temple in the same region. Hestia lets you use two types of stones on a single temple, while Hermes straight-up gives you another turn.

Hephaestus and Zeus both add extra foundation stones to your temples, and Poseidon teleports you across the map. Artemis and Aphrodite both give you a chance to collect additional glory tokens - which you can usually only acquire by building a region's tallest (or, sometimes, second-tallest) temple. It's these Glory tokens that decide the game's winner.

The gods are what turn these calm seas into surging, strategic waves. You're no longer just gunning for the island that nets you the most glory. A detour to pick up a powerful god stone could seriously change the board state, and it's worth squabbling over those pieces before they're gone. The fact each game's gods are randomized makes this tactical tempest tough to control, but it also makes this a game worth returning to for repeat plays.

Those aren't the only tricky choices you'll face. Your voyage starts gently, with enough space for everyone to build their towers. Quickly, though, the archipelago grows crowded.

You'll need to decide which Glory tokens to fight over, and what stones you're prepared to spend on that battle. A tower using all of your three-pip tokens is almost guaranteed to win, but that means fewer chances to claim land elsewhere. Plus, do you spend a god token early or late - or avoid spending them at all?

Some, like Apollo and Hermes, trigger additional draws from your bag. And, once someone cannot draw the required number of stones from their bag, end-game triggers. All other players take a final turn, and Glory points are totaled. Triggering end-game isn't a death sentence for your zealots, but it's a disadvantage that could bring your plans crashing down.

For the Gods! is an easygoing, beginner-friendly teach, but the competition is rather brutal. The gods do not suffer misplays. Take your eye off an undisputed region, dedicate at the wrong time, or mismanage your remaining bag, and it's easy to fall behind in the race for glory.

That breeds an environment of tense turns, where your decisions have real impact. The game's reliance on luck occasionally stifles this, as a bad pull from your bag can seriously slow you down. Still, it's a relatively minor frustration. The joy of this game is making the best of the limited turns, space, and stones in front of you.

It's a successful design, but for me, it's not particularly memorable. Area majority is a crowded genre, and many rivals offer more innovation, complexity, and strategic thrill. Plus, there's no clever marriage of theme and mechanics that elevates this above the many, many other Greek mythology board games. For the Gods! is gorgeous, but its theme feels superficial overall.

Those aren't deal-breakers, and I expect many people will love For the Gods! Its simplicity, style, and strategy are impressive, if not ground-breaking. Any minor deity would be happy with this offering.

Want to learn more about the year's best board games? Check out our guide, which I update weekly. Or, poke me in the Wargamer Discord and ask for some more recommendations.

A review copy was provided by the publisher.

title: Bizarre WW1 wargame starring anteaters in trenches gets a brand new starter set
content:
Quar: Clash of Rhyfles, the skirmish wargame inspired by a child's loredump, and featuring WW1-style combat between bizarre anteater-lizard creatures, has had a major facelift, as publisher Wargames Atlantic has just released a brand new starter set.

The redesigned box features the Royalist Creevish fighting the nomadic Western Arnyarans, with models for 12 infantrymen apiece, plus plenty of setting-agnostic terrain. The old beginner box was getting very hard to get hold of, so this new release, which launched Friday, October 16, is going to do wonders for making the title more accessible.

Featuring deep lore incongruous to its strange and cute models, Quar is a casual 'beer and pretzels' style skirmish game with lots of chaos and room for customization. With its narrative focus and particular whimsical-yet-gritty aesthetic, it has something in common with indie darling Turnip28, though of course one major difference is the existence of an official line of models.

The game features a 'pluck' resource system which you can spend to tweak outcomes, and an interesting action system where you don't know at the beginning of each turn how many moves you're going to be able to make. This adds an extra layer of uncertainty to proceedings.

The starter set is retailing for $99.95/£89.95 from Atlantic Games' website. It contains sprues for 12 figures per side (24 in total), the full rulebook, cheat sheets, tokens, dice, market and barricades terrain, and unit cards.

Wargames Atlantic promises more model kits for each of the factions in this box in 2027, along with the freedom-fighting Partisans. Hopefully we can see some vehicles, I want tractors dammit! It's also debuting a whole new mode of play for the game next year, with mass battles - upgrading the skirmish level gameplay into something on a bigger scale.

title: Pokémon's best rival has a new brand new card, but only in China
content:
The Pokémon TCG has just announced three full art Pokémon cards which will be exclusively available in China, and be prepared to get jealous, because there's a brand new N card among them.

Two of these cards, N's Plan and Hilda, are appearing in the Chinese version of Black Bolt and White Flare, which launches November 6 this year. We've got a fierce looking Hilda here, and an N with the blue lights of a city behind him.

The English version of N's Plan remains one of the most sought after cards in Black Bolt, though perhaps not as pricey as some fans thought it would be for one of the most popular Pokémon characters of all time - generally going for about $50-60. In my view, this one's significantly better, though your mileage may vary. It's maybe not as pretty as the original, but I like the colors and the composition more.

Alongside the Chinese Blaze Black/White Flare release is Gem Pack 7, the country's miniature booster packs that have only four cards apiece - with lots of different stamps and foil treatments. The selling point for this one, however, is an SAR version of Misty's Psyduck.

The original Misty's Psyduck SAR was beautiful, but this one is almost too cute. It features Psyduck chilling on a deckchair with a beachball, while its trainer walks up the beach to greet him. It's bound to be a sought after card for Psyduck fans and Misty fans alike - basically anyone who loves Gen 1.

Unfortunately for everyone else, historically these China-only cards have remained region-locked; it's unlikely they'll be printed in English, at least not any time soon. If you don't mind not being able to read them, you can still buy these cards on the secondary market, but it won't be cheap. Some (like the Gengar Pikachu, priced around $2,000) are among the most expensive Pokémon cards of the modern day.

As its TCG releases rapidly catch up with the baseline, China seems to be getting a rather large proportion of exclusive content. Regularly, the region gets its own unique cards, but I was particularly envious of the 30th anniversary Charizard figurine from a couple months back.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.
